data.title: Decentralization is a spectrum, not a binary switch
data.claim: Almost nothing is fully decentralized, and that's fine — most real-world systems (crypto and non-crypto) sit somewhere on a spectrum rather than being purely centralized or purely decentralized.
data.evidence: Article's own examples: a community garden may have a small steering group handling the calendar/bank account while every gardener decides freely what to grow in their plot; a crypto project may keep a fully open, tamper-proof public ledger while day-to-day decisions still flow through a handful of founders. Both are presented as normal hybrids, not failures.
data.interpretation: Reframes the useful diagnostic question away from "is this decentralized, yes or no?" toward "who holds power here, over what, and could they abuse it?" — used by the article to help a non-crypto-native audience evaluate real projects without treating "decentralized" as a binary marketing claim.
data.uncertainty: Illustrative framing from a plain-language guide, not a formal/quantified study of decentralization spectra; no named methodology or dataset behind the claim.

data.title: Priya Parker on structure and hosting spirit in gatherings
data.claim: "Gatherings crackle and flourish when real thought goes into them, when (often invisible) structure is baked into them, and when a host has the curiosity, willingness, and generosity of spirit to try."
data.evidence: Direct quotation attributed to Priya Parker, "The Art of Gathering: How We Meet and Why It Matters" (Riverhead Books, 2018), as cited in the article's References.
data.interpretation: Used in the article as the founding rationale for treating gatherings as an intentional design challenge rather than a default "find a venue, post an invite" script.
data.uncertainty: Quote reproduced as given in the article; page/edition location within the book was not independently verified for this ingestion.

data.title: KOI-net reached public beta in May 2025 and is actively maintained
data.claim: KOI-net, the network protocol and Python framework implementing RID-based federation, hit public beta in May 2025, is MIT-licensed, and is actively maintained (v2.0.7 as of May 2026, per `koi-net` on GitHub).
data.evidence: Cited to the BlockScience/koi-net GitHub repository.
data.interpretation: Supports the article's framing of KOI-net as a credible, currently-usable protocol option (not vaporware) for teams ready to move beyond ad hoc "federate by hand" sharing.
data.uncertainty: Version/maintenance status was not independently re-checked against the live repository at ingestion time; verify current version before citing externally.

data.title: ActivityPub/Mastodon federates followers but not post content (as of 2025)
data.claim: Mastodon's account-migration `Move` activity carries a user's followers (and, via exported CSV, their follows) to a new server, but as of 2025 the actual posts do not move automatically; true content portability is still being specified via the W3C Social Web Community Group's data-portability draft and the LOLA proposal.
data.evidence: Cited to Mastodon's own migration documentation and the W3C SWICG data-portability draft.
data.interpretation: Used as the article's "honest caveat" example — showing that even a working, widely-adopted federation protocol (ActivityPub) has an incomplete portability story, to temper expectations that adopting a protocol instantly solves portability too.
data.uncertainty: Standards work (W3C SWICG draft, LOLA) is explicitly in-progress and may have moved since the article's writing; status should be re-checked before being cited as current.

data.title: No legitimate service ever asks for your recovery phrase
data.claim: Anyone who reads your recovery phrase controls your wallet completely, with no bank to call and no fraud department to reverse a theft — and the single rule that defends against nearly every newcomer scam is that no legitimate wallet, exchange, or "support agent" will ever ask you to type or share it.
data.evidence: Article names three recurring scam patterns as evidence: (1) fake support agents claiming an account is "frozen" and requesting the recovery phrase to "fix" it; (2) "free-money bait" posts that publicly share a wallet's recovery phrase, tricking people into importing it and draining their own funds instead; (3) lookalike sites/apps, near-perfect copies of real wallets built to capture what's typed.
data.interpretation: Positioned as the single highest-leverage safety rule in the article — "hold that one line and you've avoided most of the danger" — because it covers all three named scam vectors at once.
data.uncertainty: General security guidance stated as settled fact in a plain-language guide; no incidence statistics or named source cited for how common each scam pattern is.

data.title: Paper is no longer a sufficient recovery-phrase backup
data.claim: Faded ink, fire, flood, and simple misplacement now rank among the leading causes of permanently lost crypto, so paper alone is no longer considered a sufficient backup for a recovery phrase.
data.evidence: Stated in the article's "Going deeper" callout, which recommends steel-plate backups (brands named: Cryptosteel, Billfodl) stored in a second, separate location, plus notes that newer passkey/guardian-based smart wallets (Base App, Argent "Ready") now offer an alternative to paper backups entirely.
data.interpretation: Used to justify recommending steel backups and/or smart-wallet recovery over plain paper, without dismissing paper as unusable, only as insufficient on its own for anything the reader would be upset to lose.
data.uncertainty: No cited statistics or named study on lost-crypto causes; the claim reads as accepted community wisdom in the source article rather than a sourced figure.

data.title: Toucan accounts for ~85% of digital carbon-credit volume
data.claim: Toucan now accounts for roughly 85% of all digital carbon credits and has supported around $4 billion in trading volume, working alongside established standards bodies like Gold Standard and Puro.earth.
data.evidence: Stated directly in the source article as a scale figure for Toucan Protocol, without an inline citation to a specific report or dashboard.
data.interpretation: Used by the article to establish Toucan as the dominant infrastructure for carbon-credit tokenization before pivoting to the Verra retired-credit controversy — i.e. scale is presented alongside a caution about quality, not as an unqualified endorsement.
data.uncertainty: No primary source or date-stamped figure is cited in the article for the 85% / $4B numbers; not independently verified here. Carbon-market volume figures are also known to shift quickly and to be reported inconsistently across trackers.

data.title: Verra banned tokenizing already-retired carbon credits (2023)
data.claim: In 2023 the standards body Verra banned converting already-retired carbon credits into tokens, after critics showed many tokenized credits were tied to old, low-quality projects that weren't genuinely helping the climate; the industry is now working toward an "immobilize, don't double-count" approach instead.
data.evidence: Stated in the source article as historical/regulatory context for Toucan and the broader carbon-tokenization space; article links to Toucan's own blog response to Verra's announcement as a reference.
data.interpretation: Article uses this as its central "honest part" — the concrete greenwashing cautionary example backing its claim that "tokenizing something does not automatically make it good."
data.uncertainty: Presented from the source article's summary and Toucan's own response-to-Verra post (one interested party's framing); the underlying Verra policy text and independent reporting on the episode were not reviewed directly here.

data.title: GG24 Bioregional Reforestation Round scale
data.claim: In GG24 (the round Gitcoin ran October 14-28, 2025 as the first round of its "Gitcoin 3.0" relaunch), the Bioregional Reforestation Round carried a $100,000 matching pool spread across nine bioregions, including Nigeria, Kenya/Uganda, Cascadia, and the Mediterranean Coast, with roughly 1,286 unique donors making about 3,042 donations, and co-funders including CeloPG, the Ethereum Foundation, the Climate Coordination Network, and the BioFi Project.
data.evidence: Cited in the article's References to "Gitcoin Grants 24 (GG24)" (https://gitcoin.co/campaigns/gitcoin-grants-24-gg24) and "Bioregional Reforestation Round" (https://gov.gitcoin.co/t/bioregional-reforestation-round/24927).
data.interpretation: Used in the article as proof that quadratic funding already routes real money to on-the-ground regenerative work, not just crypto infrastructure — offered as the concrete case a local node running tree-planting, food sovereignty, or watershed work could look to.
data.uncertainty: Donor/donation counts are approximate ("roughly," "about") as reported in the article's cited sources; not independently re-verified for this ingestion.

data.title: Gitcoin's two-layer sybil defense — Human Passport and COCM
data.claim: Gitcoin QF rounds defend against sybil attacks in two main ways: proof of personhood via Human Passport (formerly Gitcoin Passport, acquired by the Holonym Foundation in February 2025), which scores donors before their contribution counts toward matching; and post-round correction via Connection-Oriented Cluster Matching (COCM), which dials down the match for donor clusters that always co-donate together.
data.evidence: Cited in the article's References to "Human Passport (formerly Gitcoin Passport)" (https://human.tech/blog/from-gitcoin-passport-to-human-passport-we-re-now-part-of-human-tech) and "Leveling the Field: Connection-Oriented Cluster Matching" (https://www.gitcoin.co/blog/leveling-the-field-how-connection-oriented-cluster-matching-strengthens-quadratic-funding).
data.interpretation: Presented as the two things a round organizer must understand before running a round, because final allocations move after donations close as these corrections are applied.
data.uncertainty: Acquisition date and mechanism descriptions as reported in the cited Gitcoin/Human Passport sources; not independently re-verified.

data.title: Top 50 DAO treasuries hold ~$15B, concentrated in native token
data.claim: "The top 50 DAO treasuries together hold approximately $15 billion in assets. Yet most of these treasuries are heavily concentrated in a single asset: their own governance token."
data.evidence: No citation or source is given in the article itself (article frontmatter lists `sources: []`); the figure is stated as fact without a linked dataset, dashboard, or dated snapshot.
data.interpretation: Grounds the article's central argument (paper wealth vs. actual financial flexibility) but the number is undated and unsourced within the article, so its currentness cannot be verified from this text alone.
data.uncertainty: High — a specific dollar figure with no citation, dataset, or as-of date. Treasury totals in crypto move quickly; treat as illustrative rather than a verified, current statistic until a primary source is attached.

data.title: Recommendation: hold 2-3 years of operating expenses in stablecoins
data.claim: "The most practical solution: maintain 2-3 years of operating expenses in stablecoins like USDC or DAI" as a DAO treasury's survival buffer through bear markets.
data.evidence: Argued from the four stated benefits (resilience during downturns, predictable budgeting, contributor flexibility, yield/credit opportunities) — no external study, dataset, or named DAO case is cited to support the specific "2-3 years" figure.
data.interpretation: This is a concrete financial/governance recommendation a reader could act on directly (how much of a DAO's treasury to hold, and in what form) — the kind of guidance that materially affects a DAO's finances and decision-making power if followed uncritically.
data.uncertainty: The "2-3 years" figure is presented as a rule of thumb without supporting data or named precedent; appropriate runway depends heavily on a specific DAO's burn rate, revenue, and risk tolerance.

data.title: ReFi DAO's 2024 grassroots funding distribution to Local Nodes
data.claim: ReFi DAO distributed over $236,000 to grassroots communities, including its Local Nodes, through 2024 funding rounds, and ran a Local Node Incubator that put more than 100 participants through a 13-session program.
data.evidence: Cited in the article's References to "ReFi DAO, Local Nodes Showcase 2024" (https://blog.refidao.com/refi-local-nodes-showcase-2024/); no primary-source figures were independently re-verified for this ingestion.
data.interpretation: Framed in the article as evidence that direct grants are "where most local nodes actually get their first money," ahead of more exotic on-chain mechanisms.
data.uncertainty: Figures are as reported by ReFi DAO's own blog post (secondary citation, not independently verified); "over $236,000" is the article's exact wording, not a re-derived total.

data.title: Gitcoin Passport's Sybil-influence reduction and its centralization trade-off
data.claim: Gitcoin Passport (now Human Passport) scoring cut Sybil influence in quadratic-funding rounds by roughly 90%, but introduced acknowledged points of centralization, including reliance on Gitcoin's own identity tooling.
data.evidence: Cited in the article's References to "Gitcoin, Sybil Resistance in Quadratic Funding" (https://gitcoin.co/research/quadratic-funding-sybil-resistance) and "How to Attack and Defend Quadratic Funding" (https://www.gitcoin.co/blog/how-to-attack-and-defend-quadratic-funding).
data.interpretation: Used in the article as the concrete illustration of its stated principle that "every fix for Sybil resistance trades away some decentralisation for integrity."
data.uncertainty: The ~90% figure is as reported in Gitcoin's own research post (secondary citation, not independently re-derived here).

data.title: US crypto-related losses reported to the FBI hit $9.3B in 2024
data.claim: Victims reported $9.3 billion in crypto-related losses to the FBI in 2024, a 66% jump from the year before; investment fraud was the single largest category at $5.8 billion.
data.evidence: FBI 2024 Internet Crime Report (IC3), cited by URL in the article's references.
data.interpretation: Used to establish stakes before walking through specific scam types; investment-fraud share motivates the article's dedicated "too-good-to-be- true returns" section.
data.uncertainty: FBI IC3 figures rely on victim self-reporting, which undercounts actual losses (many victims don't report). Not independently re-verified against the source PDF here.

data.title: Taxonomy first, ontology later — the strong default for small-team commons
data.claim: "For a team your size, the strong default is: ship a SKOS taxonomy now, and only reach for an ontology when a specific, recurring task can't be done by hand." Ask one question to decide: does anything need to reason over your relationships, or do humans just need to find things?
data.evidence: Cited to SGKG's framing (taxonomy-as-classification vs. ontology-as- relationships, and how they layer) and Hedden Information Management's breakdown of the SKOS/OWL standards landscape; illustrated with Wikipedia's category system and Schema.org as taxonomy-scale examples vs. Wikidata as an ontology-scale example.
data.interpretation: A practical decision heuristic for the Regen Toolkit's own Layer 1 (Ontology & Semantic Kernel) posture, which the article explicitly quotes: "not to create a perfect ontology before use" but enough shared meaning to avoid silently incompatible categories.
data.uncertainty: This is editorial guidance from a knowledge-site article, not a peer-reviewed study — reasonable as a heuristic, not a proven rule for every commons.

data.title: Grassroots Economics' Sarafu network scaled from vouchers, not a token launch
data.claim: Grassroots Economics (the Kenyan nonprofit behind the Sarafu network) did not launch with a token economy — Sarafu began as community members issuing simple vouchers, and only migrated onto the Celo blockchain after the model had proven itself on the ground. The network now supports tens of thousands of small businesses across Kenya, Cameroon, and South Africa; in a 2025 survey of active users, 95% said the network is important or very important to their household economy.
data.evidence: Cited in the article's References to "Grassroots Economics, Sarafu Network" (https://www.grassrootseconomics.org/sarafu-network), "Why Celo" (https://www.grassrootseconomics.org/celo-ge), and "2025 Sarafu Network Study Results" (https://grassecon.substack.com/p/2025-sarafu-network-study-results).
data.interpretation: Used in the article as the concrete real-world example of "earning your way onto a blockchain" — the technology as an upgrade to a working community practice, never a substitute for it.
data.uncertainty: Figures (survey percentage, business counts, country coverage) as reported in Grassroots Economics' own materials; not independently re-verified for this ingestion.

data.title: Bristol Pound and Bristol Pay wound down for lack of funding, not a flawed idea
data.claim: The Bristol Pound ran a respected local currency in the UK for nearly a decade and still wound down in 2020-2021, not because the idea was wrong, but because the organization couldn't secure the funding to keep the lights on. Its successor, Bristol Pay, tried to carry the mission forward in digital form and was itself discontinued in 2023, again for lack of funding.
data.evidence: Cited in the article's References to "Bristol Pound (Wikipedia)" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bristol_pound).
data.interpretation: Used in the article as a sustainability cautionary tale — the takeaway given is "design for sustainability from week one," not "don't bother."
data.uncertainty: Sourced to a single tertiary reference (Wikipedia); dates and cause of discontinuation not independently cross-checked against primary sources for this ingestion.

data.title: Commons governance principles (Ostrom) apply to source-system stewardship
data.claim: A source system that no one is allowed to govern eventually gets trashed or abandoned; Ostrom's commons-design principles — clearly defined boundaries (who may use/change the resource) and graduated sanctions (proportionate responses to rule-breaking) — translate directly into "who can edit/add/delete" and "how to handle a contributor who keeps adding unsourced claims."
data.evidence: Cites Elinor Ostrom's Nobel-winning work on common-pool resource governance (P2P Foundation summary of her eight design principles) and the Token Engineering Commons' "Cultural Build," which explicitly builds on those same eight principles.
data.interpretation: Frames source-system stewardship as fundamentally a social/governance problem, not a tooling problem — "tools store the knowledge; stewards keep it trustworthy."
data.uncertainty: The application of Ostrom's principles (developed for physical common-pool resources like fisheries and irrigation systems) to digital knowledge commons is an analogy the article asserts rather than empirically demonstrates for this specific context.

data.title: Inclusion does not mean endorsement
data.claim: Adding a source to a knowledge commons means it is "relevant enough to preserve, classify, review, route, or revisit" — it does not mean the project vouches for or endorses its content.
data.evidence: Stated as an explicit Toolkit rule in its own reference docs [RKC], paired with the practice of recording provenance on everything so raw, unverified material can be kept without quietly becoming treated as true.
data.interpretation: This is the mechanical justification for why provenance and honest maturity labelling matter — without them, "inclusion ≠ endorsement" cannot actually hold, because readers have no way to tell reviewed material from raw inclusions.
data.uncertainty: Sourced to the toolkit's own internal reference docs via a generic placeholder URL in this article's references list — verify the actual citation target before treating this as an external, independently reviewed claim.

data.title: EAS has recorded 9.5M+ attestations as of mid-2026
data.claim: The Ethereum Attestation Service (EAS), described as the most widely used attestation tool, had recorded over 9.5 million attestations as of mid-2026.
data.evidence: Stated directly in the source article as a scale figure for EAS, without an inline citation to a live dashboard or report; article links to attest.org and the easscan.org explorer.
data.interpretation: Used to establish EAS as mature, widely-adopted infrastructure before recommending a local node attest its own events (workshops, plantings, deliverables) on it as a portable, verifiable impact record.
data.uncertainty: No primary dashboard snapshot or date-stamped source cited in the article for the 9.5M figure; attestation counts on public explorers change continuously, so this number is a point-in-time claim, not independently re-verified here.

data.title: Retroactive funding pays for demonstrated impact, not promises
data.claim: Retroactive funding (paying for work after it's done and its impact is demonstrated, rather than funding promises up front) has become a core Web3 funding pattern — popularized by Optimism's RetroPGF rounds and used in Gitcoin Grants 24 (GG24, late 2025 into 2026), which deployed six funding mechanisms at once including retroactive funding and peer-reviewed hypercerts.
data.evidence: Article states the RetroPGF logic ("easier to agree on what was useful than to predict what will be") and cites GG24's six-mechanism design as a concrete instance, without linking a primary GG24 results report.
data.interpretation: Used to argue that for a Web3-native local node, measurement is the funding rail itself, not paperwork filed after funding — "no record, no reward" is the article's summary line.
data.uncertainty: GG24 mechanism count and framing taken from the article's summary; no direct citation to Gitcoin's own GG24 results/retrospective was checked here, and "core pattern" is the article's characterization rather than a cited adoption metric.

data.title: Crypto donations to nonprofits grew 386% year-over-year in 2024
data.claim: More than $1 billion in crypto was donated to nonprofits in 2024, a 386% increase from 2023; about 70% of Forbes' Top 100 US charities now accept crypto, up from 12% in 2020.
data.evidence: Cited to The Giving Block (annual crypto-giving report).
data.source_lineage: The Giving Block 2025 Annual Report (as cited in the article)
data.interpretation: Signals rapid mainstreaming of crypto philanthropy among large US charities; article extrapolates this trend as relevant to smaller nonprofits too.
data.uncertainty: Figures are taken at face value from the article; the underlying Giving Block report was not independently checked, and The Giving Block is a commercial platform with an incentive to report favorable growth.

data.title: Mercy Corps Ventures cut delivery costs 60% using stablecoins in Syria
data.claim: Mercy Corps Ventures cut delivery costs by 60% by using stablecoins instead of traditional money transfers in Syria.
data.evidence: Cited to cryptoaltruism.org (CryptoAltruists Web3 Impact Toolkit).
data.source_lineage: CryptoAltruists Web3 Impact Toolkit (as cited in the article)
data.interpretation: Used as the article's concrete "everyday operations" proof point for stablecoins beyond emergency crisis fundraising.
data.uncertainty: Single-source figure with no methodology given for how the 60% cost reduction was calculated; not independently verified here.

data.title: Bitcoin's proof-of-work energy use: ~138 TWh/year (Cambridge, 2025)
data.claim: Bitcoin secures itself via proof of work "using on the order of 138 terawatt-hours a year (Cambridge, 2025), comparable to a mid-sized country."
data.evidence: Attributed to the Cambridge Bitcoin Electricity Consumption Index, an independent, regularly updated estimate maintained by the University of Cambridge, linked in the article's references.
data.source_lineage: src/content/docs/what-is-blockchain.md — Cambridge Bitcoin Electricity Consumption Index (https://ccaf.io/cbnsi/cbeci)
data.interpretation: Used to ground the "energy" honesty section — contrasted directly with Ethereum's post-Merge proof-of-stake energy use to show the claim "blockchain wastes energy" does not generalize across consensus mechanisms.
data.uncertainty: Cambridge's index is a continuously updated estimate, not a fixed figure — "on the order of 138 TWh" should be treated as a snapshot (dated 2025 per the article) that will drift over time; verify against the live index before citing a precise number.

data.title: Ethereum's Merge cut energy use by ~99.95%
data.claim: "On 15 September 2022, Ethereum ... switched to proof of stake, which secures the chain through deposited funds rather than raw computing, and cut its energy use by about 99.95% overnight."
data.evidence: Attributed to Ethereum.org's official account of "The Merge," linked in the article's references.
data.interpretation: Central to the article's argument that "blockchain wastes energy" is outdated for the networks (Ethereum, Celo) most regenerative projects actually build on.
data.uncertainty: The 99.95% figure and date are well-documented and widely corroborated for Ethereum's own transition; not independently re-verified here beyond the cited official source.

data.title: Walmart mango traceback dropped from ~7 days to 2.2 seconds on Hyperledger Fabric
data.claim: "In a pilot tracing mangoes, finding a fruit's origin dropped from about seven days to 2.2 seconds" using Hyperledger Fabric.
data.evidence: Attributed to the LF Decentralized Trust Walmart case study, linked in the article's references.
data.source_lineage: src/content/docs/what-is-blockchain.md — LF Decentralized Trust: Walmart case study (https://www.lfdecentralizedtrust.org/case-studies/walmart-case-study)
data.interpretation: Used as the enterprise-scale comparison point for how a shared, checkable record turns a contamination-scare investigation from days of guesswork into a same-minute answer.
data.uncertainty: Pilot-result figures reported by the platform steward's own case study; not independently re-verified against Walmart's own disclosures here.

data.title: Grassroots Economics' Sarafu Network scale (26,000+ people, ~290 communities)
data.claim: "Grassroots Economics reports the network has supported more than 26,000 people across roughly 290 communities, with thousands now coordinating through Celo-based 'commitment pools.'"
data.evidence: Attributed to Grassroots Economics' own Sarafu Network page, linked in the article's references — a self-reported figure by the project steward.
data.interpretation: Used as the article's lead real-world example of blockchain-enabled community currency reaching people without smartphones (via USSD/basic phones), grounding the "trustless" and "immutable" concepts in a live deployment.
data.uncertainty: Self-reported by the project steward (Grassroots Economics), not an independently audited figure; treat as the organization's own claim about its reach rather than third-party-verified impact data.

data.title: Regen Network's on-chain ecological data lets a distant funder trust regeneration happened
data.claim: "Regen Network pays land stewards for measurable ecological work, like restored soil or biodiversity, by recording verified ecological data on a blockchain and issuing credits that buyers can purchase. The shared, checkable record is what lets a funder half a world away trust that the regeneration actually happened."
data.evidence: Described at a high level in the article with a link to Regen Network's own site; no specific MRV (measurement/reporting/verification) methodology, dataset, or third-party audit is cited or described in the source text itself.
data.interpretation: This is an ecological/MRV-adjacent claim (a standing high-risk trigger per the ingest skill) about what an on-chain record can vouch for ("the regeneration actually happened"). The blockchain guarantees tamper-evidence of whatever data was recorded — it does not by itself verify that the underlying ecological measurement was accurate; the article does not separate these two claims.
data.uncertainty: High for the ecological-outcome portion of the claim: the article asserts trust is warranted but does not describe Regen Network's actual MRV methodology, verifier credentials, or audit process. The tamper-evidence portion (blockchain records are checkable) is on firmer ground than the implied ecological-accuracy portion.

data.title: ReFi DAO has supported 100+ events across 58 cities
data.claim: ReFi DAO has supported 100+ events across 58 cities through its local-node network.
data.evidence: Stated in the article as a scale indicator for the ReFi DAO local-node network; not attributed to a specific dated report.
data.interpretation: Used to establish that ReFi DAO coordinates a real, sizeable network, supporting the article's recommendation to plug into an existing network rather than build alone.
data.uncertainty: No specific source or as-of date is given for this figure in the article; treat as an approximate, unverified network-scale claim.

data.title: Regen Coordination distributed $236,000+ to communities across 2024
data.claim: Across 2024, Regen Coordination programs distributed over $236,000 to regenerative communities, and the Local Node Incubator ran 13 sessions with over 100 participants. Separately, ReFi Medellín raised roughly $4,000 in Gitcoin Grants 17 (March 2023).
data.evidence: Cited to ReFi DAO Wrapped 2024 (blog.refidao.com) and the Bízková interview on ReFi Medellín's Gitcoin Grants 17 experience.
data.source_lineage: ReFi DAO Wrapped 2024 (https://blog.refidao.com/refi-dao-wrapped-2024/) ; Gitcoin Grants & ReFi Medellín interview with Tereza Bízková
data.interpretation: Used as evidence that real funding flows through this network, but the article frames it as accruing to nodes that have already proven they convene people and ship events — not as money available on demand.
data.uncertainty: Figures taken from the article's citations at face value; underlying reports were not independently re-checked at ingestion time. This is organizational funding-distribution data, which the framework treats as high-risk-by-default even when the source is a public wrap-up post.

data.title: Polished writing is not automatically reviewed knowledge
data.claim: "Polished writing is not automatically reviewed knowledge" — readers cannot distinguish a beautifully written unreviewed draft from a fact-checked, reviewed page unless the review state is explicitly labelled.
data.evidence: Named as one of the Regen Web3 Toolkit's own cross-cutting principles (Maturity and review state), illustrated by the article's opening example of a confident-looking but unreviewed treasury-payout page.
data.interpretation: Argues for mandatory, visible maturity labelling (not just internal metadata) as the cheap fix — a badge at the top of the page, not a footnote.
data.uncertainty: Editorial/design guidance rather than an empirically tested claim; the treasury-payout scenario is illustrative, not a documented incident.

data.title: Token concentration can negate sociopolitical decentralization
data.claim: In blockchain systems, token holdings often determine sociopolitical power; a system where one wallet controls 50% of tokens is not truly decentralized regardless of its technical architecture.
data.evidence: Asserted directly in the article as an illustrative example, not tied to a specific named blockchain or on-chain data source.
data.source_lineage: src/content/docs/decentralization-spectrum.md (author's own framing; no external citation given)
data.interpretation: Central to the article's "two dimensions" argument — used to show that technological decentralization (node count/distribution) and sociopolitical decentralization (who actually controls decisions/value) must be assessed separately.
data.uncertainty: The 50%-single-wallet example is illustrative/general rather than backed by a cited case or dataset; no specific chain or holder analysis is referenced. Treat as a reasoned claim, not an empirically sourced one.

data.title: A private key exclusively controls signing authority over a blockchain account
data.claim: "Your private key has the power to control your entire account. This allows you to make decisions on the blockchain, or in other words, sign transactions."
data.evidence: Direct quotation attributed to "[Source S]" in how-transactions-work.md's "Signing" step, which the article's References section identifies as Ledger Academy: How Does a Blockchain Transaction Work.
data.interpretation: Used to explain why a private key must never be shared — it is the sole mechanism proving transaction authorization.
data.uncertainty: Quote reproduced as given in the article; exact wording was not independently checked against the live Ledger Academy page for this ingestion.

data.title: Once included in a block, a transaction becomes an immutable part of blockchain history

data.evidence: Direct quotation attributed to "[Source S]" in how-transactions-work.md's "Confirmation" step, which the article's References section identifies as Ledger Academy: How Does a Blockchain Transaction Work.

data.title: Fukuyama: social trust underwrites low-cost economic cooperation
data.claim: Political scientist Francis Fukuyama argued in "Trust" (1995) that social trust is the foundation of economic cooperation: high-trust groups coordinate complex activity at low cost, while low-trust groups need expensive enforcement and bureaucracy.
data.evidence: Cited in the article from Fukuyama, "Trust: The Social Virtues and the Creation of Prosperity" (Free Press, 1995), listed in the article's References.
data.interpretation: Used as the article's foundational argument for treating trust, not verification technology, as the real infrastructure of community finance — reframed as a blunt diagnostic question: "are you building social trust, or substituting technology for trust you have not earned yet?"
data.uncertainty: Reproduces the article's own characterization of Fukuyama's 1995 thesis; not independently re-verified against the book's full argument for this ingestion.

data.title: 95% of surveyed Sarafu users called it important to their household (2025)
data.claim: A 2025 survey of 855 active Sarafu Network users found 95% called it important to their household, with the most common reason being that it gave them a way to give and receive help in their community.
data.evidence: Cited in the article, attributed to Grassroots Economics' own reporting on the Sarafu Network, listed in the article's References (grassrootseconomics.org/sarafu-network).
data.interpretation: Used as the article's concrete evidence that a trust-based commitment- pooling system can work at real scale, supporting the article's broader claim that "the chain records the promises. The neighbors keep them."
data.uncertainty: The survey's full methodology (sampling method, question wording, margin of error) is not detailed in the article itself; the 855-user sample and 95% figure are reproduced as cited, not independently re-verified against Grassroots Economics' primary survey data for this ingestion.

data.title: Eating together more often correlates with trust, happiness, and community engagement
data.claim: People who eat socially more often report trusting others more, feeling happier, and being more engaged with their local community, and the causal arrow runs from eating together to bonding, not the reverse — used to justify the community-meal gathering format as the foundational trust-building layer for a local node.
data.evidence: Cited to Dunbar, "Breaking Bread: The Functions of Social Eating" (2017), described as a UK survey study, linked in the article's references (https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40750-017-0061-4).
data.interpretation: Used to justify prioritizing informal, food-based gatherings before introducing any web3/governance concept to a new local-node community.
data.uncertainty: The article asserts a specific causal direction ("the causal arrow runs from eating together to bonding, not the reverse") as settled from a single UK survey study; a single correlational-plus-directional claim from one study should be treated as suggestive rather than definitive, and the study's UK-specific sample may not generalize to all local-node contexts globally.

data.title: Walking substantially boosts creative idea generation over sitting
data.claim: In a set of Stanford experiments, between 81% and 100% of participants (depending on the specific test) produced more creative ideas while walking than while sitting, indoors or outdoors, and walkers roughly doubled their novel responses — used to justify the walk-and-talk gathering format for brainstorming and processing difficult conversations.
data.evidence: Cited to Oppezzo & Schwartz, "Give Your Ideas Some Legs" (APA, 2014), linked in the article's references (https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2014/04/creativity-walk).
data.interpretation: Used to justify the walk-and-talk format specifically for brainstorming and for lowering the intensity of hard one-on-one conversations (side-by-side positioning reduces eye-contact pressure).
data.uncertainty: The article's own reading is careful ("the walking itself did the work, not the scenery"), but it does not specify which of the study's multiple conditions/tests produced the 81% vs 100% range, so the precise figure per condition is not verifiable from this article alone.

data.title: Ethereum secures $410B+ in value and cut energy use ~99% via the 2022 Merge
data.claim: Ethereum "secures over $410 billion in value and hosts thousands of projects"; in September 2022 it switched consensus mechanisms and reduced its energy use by roughly 99%.
data.evidence: Stated directly in the article body, attributed in the References section to ethereum.org's "What is Ethereum?" and general Ethereum.org documentation; no specific dated source cited for the $410B figure itself.
data.interpretation: Used to (a) establish scale/legitimacy for a skeptical newcomer audience and (b) preempt the standard "crypto wastes energy" objection before introducing smart contracts and DAOs.
data.uncertainty: The $410B TVL/market-cap-style figure is inherently time-sensitive (crypto valuations move daily to monthly) and no snapshot date or source link is given for it specifically, unlike the well-documented ~99% energy-reduction figure from The Merge (Sept 2022), which is independently well-sourced elsewhere. Treat the dollar figure as illustrative-at-time-of-writing, not a stable fact.

data.title: Grazing-land recovery example: rest-rotation grazing confirmed by satellite
data.claim: Community members documented grass regrowth in previously degraded grazing areas, proving that their rest-rotation grazing practice was working; satellite verification confirmed their observations.
data.evidence: Presented in the article as "Example 3: Grazing Land Recovery," an illustrative case combining community documentation with satellite verification.
data.interpretation: Used to demonstrate the "automated + human verification" pattern in dMRV, and to show an ecological/impact claim being validated through a combination of local observation and remote sensing.
data.uncertainty: Presented as an illustrative example without a named location, date, organization, or citable data source — likely a composite/generic scenario rather than a specific, independently verifiable case; treat as an ecological/impact claim requiring domain review before any decision-relevant reuse.

data.title: Outdated documentation can cause harm
data.claim: Documentation is only valuable if it stays current — outdated documentation can actually cause harm because people make decisions based on wrong information.

data.title: ReFi DAO's alpha-cohort Local Node Incubator supported 30-plus events and raised ~$55k via Gitcoin
data.claim: "ReFi DAO... runs an eight-week Local Node Incubator. Its alpha cohort supported 30-plus local events and helped nodes raise about $55k through featured rounds on Gitcoin Grants." data.title: Compound DAO's Proposal 289 shows low turnout can enable treasury capture
data.claim: On 28 July 2024, a delegate bloc nicknamed the "Golden Boys" passed Compound DAO Proposal 289 (moving 499,000 COMP, ~$24M, from the treasury into a vault they controlled) by amassing enough delegated COMP to clear quorum while most of the community stayed home (682,191 vs 633,636 votes); the proposal was rescinded days later under community pressure.
data.evidence: Cited to contemporaneous CoinDesk and Cointelegraph reporting on the proposal and its rescission.
data.interpretation: Used as the article's central cautionary example that sophisticated on-chain governance tooling does not by itself produce legitimacy — DAO voter turnout across most DAOs sits below 10% (Uniswap often 2-3%), which concentrates effective power in whoever bothers to show up.
data.uncertainty: Figures (vote counts, COMP amount, USD value) are as reported by the cited press sources at the time; USD value of COMP fluctuates with market price.

data.title: As of 2022: 215+ DAOs managed ~$9.5B with ~500,000 active members
data.claim: As of 2022, over 215 DAOs collectively managed around $9.5 billion with approximately 500,000 active members.

data.title: SuperBenefit's Knowledge Garden sorts content into raw, working, and refined-artifact tiers
data.claim: SuperBenefit structures its Knowledge Garden into tiers — raw notes, working documents, and refined "artifacts" — as a working example of content sorted by review/consequence state.

data.title: Ithaca Hours, Bristol Pound, and Brixton Pound declined after single-steward dependency

data.title: Sarafu Network supports 26,000+ people across ~290 Kenyan communities
data.claim: Sarafu Network, run by the Kenyan nonprofit Grassroots Economics, supports 26,000+ people across roughly 290 communities using commitment pools (shared accounts where members issue Community Asset Vouchers) and runs on the Celo blockchain via USSD, so it works on basic phones without internet.

data.title: Ethereum's Merge cut network energy use by roughly 99.95%
data.claim: Ethereum's September 2022 switch from proof-of-work to proof-of-stake ("The Merge") cut the network's energy use by roughly 99.95%, meaning the honest answer to "is crypto bad for the environment" depends entirely on which network and consensus method a project is built on, not on crypto as a monolith.
data.evidence: Article cites ethereum.org's own Merge explainer for the ~99.95% figure, and separately cites the Cambridge Centre for Alternative Finance's Bitcoin Electricity Consumption Index (~140-175 TWh/year) as the contrasting proof-of-work baseline.
data.interpretation: Used to reframe an all-or-nothing question ("is crypto clean or dirty") into a design-choice question ("which consensus method does this specific network use") — Ethereum and Celo (proof-of-stake) vs. Bitcoin (proof-of-work).
data.uncertainty: Figures are drawn from the cited primary sources (ethereum.org, Cambridge CBECI) but not independently re-verified here; CBECI's Bitcoin estimate is itself a range/model, not a single hard measurement.

data.title: Global remittance fees average far more than crypto rails would cost
data.claim: Sending $200 abroad cost a global average of 6.36% in fees in late 2025, and averaged nearly 15% through a bank specifically, making cheap crypto-based transfers matter most to people with the least, not a luxury for the wealthy.
data.evidence: Cited to the World Bank's Remittance Prices Worldwide quarterly dataset.
data.interpretation: Used to rebut the "crypto is only for rich people" concern by pointing at who actually bears high fees today: low-income remittance senders.
data.uncertainty: Global average masks large variation by corridor and provider; article does not cite the specific corridor(s) measured for the ~15% bank figure.

data.title: Ethereum's 2022 Merge cut network energy use by about 99.95% overnight
data.claim: Bitcoin's proof-of-work consensus consumes roughly as much electricity each year as a small country like Norway, but Ethereum's 2022 switch to proof of stake cut its electricity use by about 99.95% overnight, and most newer chains (including Celo, used by the Sarafu Network and Regen Network examples in this article) work the low-energy proof-of-stake way — so "crypto wrecks the climate" is largely a Bitcoin-specific story, not a crypto-wide one.
data.evidence: Cited to ethereum.org's official Merge account for the ~99.95% figure, and to the Cambridge Bitcoin Electricity Consumption Index for the Bitcoin/Norway energy comparison, both listed in the article's references.
data.interpretation: Used directly to answer the "isn't this terrible for the planet?" fear by reframing an all-or-nothing question into a chain-specific, design-choice question.
data.uncertainty: Figures are drawn from the cited primary sources but not independently re-verified in this article; the Cambridge index's Bitcoin estimate is itself a range/model rather than a single hard measurement, as it is for the near-identical claim already ingested from common-concerns.md.

data.title: Traditional remittances cost ~6% on average; stable-digital-dollar rails cost a cent or two
data.claim: Sending money home through a traditional money-transfer service costs about 6% of the amount on average worldwide (and often more), according to the World Bank, while a stable digital dollar sent on a low-cost network can cost a cent or two — a meaningful gap for diaspora communities and cross-border solidarity funds.
data.evidence: Cited to the World Bank's Remittance Prices Worldwide dataset, linked in the article's references (remittanceprices.worldbank.org).
data.interpretation: Used to make the "why this might matter for your work" case concrete — reframing crypto's cost advantage as relevant to real diaspora/solidarity cross-border transfers rather than abstract finance.
data.uncertainty: "About 6%" is a global average masking large corridor-to-corridor variation; the "a cent or two" figure for stable-digital-dollar transfer is illustrative and network/fee-condition dependent, not sourced to a specific transaction example.

data.title: Universities have experimented with blockchain-based diplomas

data.title: Communities collapse when key leaders leave without succession

data.title: Wikipedia Good Article process requires a reviewer citation spot-check
data.claim: To pass Wikipedia's Good Article process, an article must cite reliable sources inline for anything that could reasonably be challenged, and the reviewer does a spot-check — sampling citations and confirming each source actually supports the sentence it's attached to.

data.title: Ethereum's move to proof-of-stake cut energy use ~99.95%
data.claim: Ethereum and the networks most regenerative projects use (Ethereum, Polygon, Arbitrum) run on proof-of-stake, which cut Ethereum's energy use by about 99.95% when it switched over ("the Merge") in September 2022 — so holding/using a seed phrase carries negligible energy cost.
data.evidence: Article cites Ethereum Foundation's official Merge/energy roadmap page (ethereum.org/en/roadmap/merge/) for the ~99.95% figure and September 2022 date.
data.interpretation: Used in the article to address a permaculture/climate-work reader's worry that crypto is inherently energy-intensive; the claim is scoped to proof-of-stake chains, not Bitcoin.
data.uncertainty: Figure and date are as stated by the cited Ethereum Foundation source; not independently re-verified in this ingestion pass. Polygon/Arbitrum being "proof-of-stake" is stated as a blanket claim without per-chain sourcing.

data.title: Bank/wire cross-border transfers can lose 6%+ to fees vs. crypto
data.claim: Sending money internationally through banks or services like Western Union can lose 6% or more to fees, and small grassroots projects often can't easily open accounts, whereas crypto can move value to a wallet in minutes for a much smaller cost.
data.evidence: Stated in how-to-get-crypto.md's "Why this might actually matter for your work" section as the article's core cross-border-cost rationale for considering crypto at all.
data.interpretation: Used to justify why a grassroots/community organization might adopt crypto for receiving grants or donations despite the article's own scam-risk warnings.
data.uncertainty: The "6% or more" figure and "much smaller cost" framing are asserted without a cited source, exact fee comparison, or date; remittance and on/off-ramp fees vary significantly by corridor, amount, and provider.

data.title: Gitcoin GG24 round (Oct-Nov 2025) distributed over $1.8 million

data.title: ReFi DAO's GG18 Local Node round: $30k pool, 18 new nodes, 1,550+ contributions

data.title: Optimism's Retro Funding thesis: "easier to agree on what was useful than what will be useful"
data.claim: Optimism's Retroactive Public Goods Funding pays projects for public goods they shipped in the past rather than for promised future work; the thesis (from the 2021 post introducing the idea, with Vitalik Buterin as guest author of the key section) is "it's easier to agree on what was useful than what will be useful."
data.evidence: Cited to "Optimism, Retroactive Public Goods Funding" (Medium, July 20, 2021, with Vitalik Buterin as guest author of the core section) in the article's References.
data.interpretation: Used to establish the second of the article's "two kinds of grants" distinction — retroactive grants require documenting delivered impact with metrics, never aspirational language, which changes what a proposal contains.
data.uncertainty: Direct paraphrase/quotation of a named, dated, attributable source (a 2021 Optimism blog post); low uncertainty on attribution, though the article does not link the live OP Atlas Retro Funding program details beyond naming atlas.optimism.io/missions as a reference.

data.title: A buddy system measurably improves newcomer onboarding satisfaction and retention
data.claim: Pairing each newcomer with one existing member as a "buddy" measurably raises onboarding satisfaction and retention: Microsoft's internal onboarding-buddy program found new hires with a buddy were 23% more satisfied with onboarding in their first week, rising to 36% more satisfied by 90 days; separately, a membership-sector analysis puts members who don't engage in their first 90 days at 60-70% more likely to be gone by renewal.
data.evidence: Article cites: Microsoft, "Every New Employee Needs an Onboarding Buddy" (techcommunity.microsoft.com, internal HR study, 23%→36% figures); i4a, "90-Day New Member Onboarding" (i4a.com, membership-sector data behind the 60-70% figure); VolunteerHub, "Onboarding for Retention" (volunteerhub.com, the "leave knowing one person's name" retention pattern).
data.interpretation: Used to justify the buddy system as "the single highest-leverage move" for local-node onboarding, and to support treating the first-90-days window as the critical retention period.
data.uncertainty: The article itself explicitly flags this: "Treat the exact percentages as directional, not gospel (they come from corporate HR contexts)." The Microsoft and i4a figures are drawn from corporate/membership-association contexts, not volunteer-run regenerative-finance local nodes specifically, so the magnitude may not transfer even if the direction is sound.

data.title: Comparative TPS and typical fees across five chains (Ethereum L1, Base, Arbitrum, Solana, Polygon)
data.claim: Approximate transactions-per-second and typical fees: Ethereum L1 15-30 TPS / $1-$100+ fees; Base (L2) ~80-90 TPS / $0.01-$0.10; Arbitrum up to 40,000 TPS / $0.01-$0.10; Solana up to 65,000 TPS / under $0.001; Polygon ~1,000 TPS / low fees.
data.evidence: Presented as a summary table in the article body; the References section points to Ethereum.org's Layer 2 page and L2Beat as general sources, but no per-chain citation or as-of date is given for the specific TPS/fee numbers.
data.interpretation: Used to make the trilemma tradeoffs concrete and to support the article's use-case-to-chain mapping (high-value DeFi → Ethereum L1; general apps → Layer 2s; high-volume consumer apps → Solana; gaming → Polygon).

Treat as illustrative-at-time-of-writing and verify current figures via L2Beat or the chains' own dashboards before using this table for a real decision.

data.title: Ethereum (2015) was the first blockchain capable of running smart contracts
data.claim: Nick Szabo coined the term "smart contract" in 1994, but the technology did not exist until Ethereum launched in 2015 as the first blockchain capable of running programs like this.
data.evidence: Asserted directly in the article's opening section; article's References list Ethereum Foundation documentation (ethereum.org) generally, not a specific citation tied to this historical claim.
data.interpretation: Establishes the historical grounding for why smart contracts are treated as a distinct, comparatively recent (2015-onward) technology.
data.uncertainty: Widely-repeated history in the Ethereum ecosystem; not independently re-verified against primary sources in this ingestion pass.

data.title: 2-of-3 multisig is vulnerable; 3-of-5 recommended for community treasuries
data.claim: "Threshold set too low" is named as the first common mistake: a 2-of-3 multisig is vulnerable because if any two signers collude or become unavailable, funds are at risk or inaccessible; the article recommends 3-of-5 or higher for community treasuries, and states "the threshold should be more than half the signers, but less than all of them."
data.evidence: Presented as the article's own security reasoning/best-practice guidance, not attributed to an external audit, incident dataset, or named case of an actual 2-of-3 multisig failure.
data.interpretation: Sound, widely-accepted operational-security logic (more signers reduces single/dual-point-of-failure risk) but stated as general best practice rather than backed by a cited incident study; the specific numeric thresholds (2-of-3 vs 3-of-5 vs 4-of-7) are heuristics, not derived from a named risk model.
data.uncertainty: Low for the qualitative principle (higher, majority-but-not-unanimous thresholds reduce risk — well-established in multisig/threshold- cryptography practice); moderate for the specific "3-of-5 is the sensible default" recommendation, which is asserted rather than evidenced against community-size or treasury-size data.

data.title: "The Web3 community is remarkably generous with time and knowledge"
data.claim: "The Web3 community is remarkably generous with time and knowledge." Framed as the closing encouragement to reach out and ask for help.
data.evidence: No citation, study, or specific example is given in the article; it is presented as the author's own observation/encouragement.

data.title: 95% of Sarafu users called the network important to their household economy (2025 survey)
data.claim: In Grassroots Economics' 2025 survey of the Sarafu community-currency network in Kenya, 95% of users called the network important or very important to their household economy.
data.evidence: Cited to "Grassroots Economics, 2025 survey" (grassecon.substack.com/p/ 2025-sarafu-network-study-results) in the article's References.
data.interpretation: Used as the article's grounded, non-speculative example of "ownership that stays local" — money designed to circulate rather than be flipped for profit — as a contrast to the article's opening warning about crypto speculation and scams.

data.title: Global average cross-border remittance cost was 6.36% in late 2025 (banks averaging 14.99%)
data.claim: "The World Bank found the global average cost of sending money across borders was 6.36% in late 2025, with banks averaging 14.99%, roughly five times the United Nations' 3% target."

In practice: (1) an attestation being "unchangeable" refers to the record of the claim, not the truth of the claim — a false or mistaken attestation is just as permanently recorded as a true one; (2) revocation schemes exist precisely because issuers sometimes need to invalidate an attestation; (3) "cannot be faked" depends entirely on trusting whoever the issuing party is, which the article does not address. The article's own `sources: []` frontmatter field confirms no supporting citation was attached.

data.title: Aragon's 2023 treasury dissolution shows unilateral structural moves can break DAO trust even when 'winning'
data.claim: In 2023, investors bought up ANT tokens to force a payout of Aragon's ~$200M treasury, which Aragon's team called a "51% attack" by "risk-free- value raiders." data.title: Algorithmic/unpaid contributor-reward models produced burnout and quiet capture in SourceCred and Gitcoin

data.evidence: Cited to Ellie Rennie's ethnography of the SourceCred CredSperiment and Gitcoin's own 2025 Governance Manual describing the revamp.
data.interpretation: Used as the article's cautionary example for "the slow-burn conflict": bolting a rewards algorithm or unpaid-but-powerful role onto a group that has not first agreed what it values corrodes trust gradually rather than exploding.
data.uncertainty: Drawn from two secondary sources (an academic-style ethnography and the organization's own retrospective framing of its revamp), not independently cross-verified against other participant accounts.

data.uncertainty: Reproduces the article's own paraphrase of Wasserman's research; the precise share of failures attributed to founder conflict is described in the article only as "a large share," not a specific cited percentage. Not independently verified against the book for this ingestion.

data.title: Ambiguous role expectations are a fast route to DAO contributor burnout
data.claim: Other Internet's "Web3 Work" research, which interviewed long-tenured full-time DAO contributors, found the fastest route to burnout is contributors working "without specific working hours/days nor clear outlines for what is expected from them" inside an always-online culture; the same report found people are drawn into DAOs by "a desire for collaboration" and aligned relationships more than by tokens or tech.
data.evidence: Cited in the article from Other Internet's "Web3 Work research report," listed in the article's References with a link to the Substack post.
data.interpretation: Used by the article to argue for naming roles out loud and recruiting for shared purpose and reliability first, since ambiguity (not workload itself) is framed as the primary burnout driver.
data.uncertainty: Direct quotations reproduced as given in the article; the underlying interview sample size/methodology is not detailed in the article itself, and was not independently verified for this ingestion.

data.title: Recommended governance sequencing — consent-based first, then quadratic voting and delegation
data.claim: "Start with consent-based decision making for small groups. As you grow, introduce quadratic voting for resource allocation and delegation for routine decisions. Review and iterate quarterly."
data.evidence: Presented as the article's own closing design recommendation, following from its stated design principles (match mechanism to context, minimize complexity, build in safeguards, iterate, transparency); no external case study or citation is given for this specific sequencing.
data.source_lineage: src/content/docs/governance-mechanism-design.md (sources listed generically as "Mechanism design theory," "DAO governance patterns," "Quadratic voting research" — no specific citations)
data.interpretation: A governance-design recommendation intended to be applied directly by a reader standing up or evolving a DAO's decision-making process — this is exactly the "governance recs" category the ingest skill flags as high-risk, since a group could adopt this sequencing as prescriptive advice for their specific context without independent review.
data.uncertainty: No empirical backing (case studies, adoption data, or citations) is given for why this particular sequence works better than alternatives; treat as one reasonable design pattern, not a validated best practice. The article's own frontmatter marks its status as "draft."

data.title: Crypto-donation platform setup takes about an hour
data.claim: Setting up to receive crypto donations "takes about an hour with most platforms," with the hardest part being gathering nonprofit verification documents.
data.evidence: Asserted directly by the article's "Bottom Line" section; no external citation or platform-by-platform timing data given.
data.interpretation: A rough operational estimate meant to lower the perceived barrier to entry for nonprofits considering crypto donations.
data.uncertainty: Self-reported estimate with no supporting data or named platform benchmarks; likely varies significantly by platform and by how quickly an org can produce nonprofit-status documentation.

data.title: IRS treats cryptocurrency as property, enabling charitable-deduction treatment like cash or stock
data.claim: In the United States, nonprofits can legally accept cryptocurrency donations; the IRS treats cryptocurrency as property, so donors can claim charitable deductions similar to cash or stock donations. Laws vary by country, and the article recommends checking local regulations or a nonprofit lawyer.
data.evidence: Attributed in-article to "CryptoAltruists" as the source.
data.interpretation: Presented as general US-context legal/tax orientation for a nonprofit deciding whether to accept crypto, not as jurisdiction-specific legal advice.
data.uncertainty: Single secondary source (CryptoAltruists, a donation-platform-adjacent resource hub, not a primary IRS citation); tax law changes over time and varies by country — the article itself flags this and recommends professional legal counsel.

data.title: Donating appreciated crypto directly can avoid US donor capital gains tax
data.claim: For US donors, donating appreciated crypto directly (rather than selling then donating cash) can mean no capital gains tax owed, and donors can deduct the full fair market value; for the receiving organization, charitable donations generally are not subject to income tax.
data.evidence: Attributed in-article to "CryptoAltruists" as the source.
data.interpretation: Used to explain why crypto donations can be more tax-advantageous than cash for a donor, and reassure orgs about their own tax exposure.
data.uncertainty: Same single secondary source as the property-treatment claim; jurisdiction- and individual-situation-specific in practice — not verified against a primary IRS source here.

data.title: Group-size-to-governance-model comparison table
data.claim: The article's comparison table maps group size to model: Collective fits 5-10 people (no legal protection, no setup effort, slow decisions); Working Groups fit 10-30 (low setup, medium speed); Council fits 20-50+ (medium/high formality, fast decisions); Cooperative fits 15+ (high formality, high setup effort, legal protection, medium decision speed).
data.evidence: Presented as the article's own synthesized guidance table, not attributed to a study, survey, or dataset of actual ReFi/DAO nodes — the ReFi DAO Steward Council and Network Initiatives examples support the qualitative descriptions but not the specific numeric size bands.
data.interpretation: A practitioner heuristic useful for a rough first cut at "which model fits us," but the size bands overlap (e.g. Cooperative "15+" overlaps Working Groups "10-30" and Council "20-50+") and are not derived from a cited comparative study of local-node governance transitions.
data.uncertainty: High for the precise numeric bands (authorial heuristic, overlapping ranges); low for the qualitative ordering (Collective → Working Groups → Council → Cooperative as increasing formality), which is well-reasoned within the article.

data.title: Crypto is property, not currency, for US tax purposes
data.claim: Crypto is treated as property, not currency, for US tax purposes, so every transaction can potentially trigger a taxable event, similar to stocks or real estate.
data.evidence: Stated as the article's foundational premise ("The Short Version"); aligns with widely reported IRS guidance (IRS Notice 2014-21 classifies virtual currency as property), though that notice is not directly cited in the article's text.
data.interpretation: Frames every subsequent taxable/non-taxable event distinction in the article.
data.uncertainty: Widely accepted characterization of current US tax treatment as of the article's writing; not independently re-verified against primary IRS guidance in this ingestion pass, and subject to future regulatory change (article itself notes "the rules are evolving").

data.title: Form 1099-DA is a new broker-reporting form starting 2025+
data.claim: Form 1099-DA is a new IRS form, applicable from 2025 onward, that brokers will send to report digital-asset transactions.
data.evidence: Stated in the article's "IRS Forms You'll Need" section; no external citation given.
data.interpretation: Presented as an upcoming compliance change readers should be aware of alongside existing forms (8949, Schedule D, Schedule 1).
data.uncertainty: Regulatory-rollout detail; not independently re-verified against current IRS guidance in this ingestion pass — broker-reporting requirements for digital assets have been subject to phased implementation and possible delay/change.

data.title: Ethereum Foundation ESP explicitly supports community events and hubs
data.claim: "The Ethereum Foundation Ecosystem Support Program explicitly supports community events and has run requests for proposals to establish permanent community hubs."
data.evidence: Cited to esp.ethereum.foundation in the article's References list.
data.interpretation: Consistent with ESP's known public-goods/ecosystem-grant remit; the specific claim about "requests for proposals to establish permanent community hubs" is a program-history detail that changes over time as ESP runs new RFPs.
data.uncertainty: Program specifics (whether a community-hub RFP is currently open, funding amounts, deadlines) are time-sensitive and were not independently verified against the live ESP site at ingestion time; check esp.ethereum.foundation directly before advising a node to apply.

data.title: DAOs collectively manage $30B+ across 13,000+ organizations
data.claim: Together, DAOs now manage over $30 billion in collective assets across more than 13,000 organizations globally.
data.evidence: Stated directly in the article's "The Big Picture" section, framed as context for why the tooling ecosystem matters; article's reference list cites Yellow.com's "2025 Platform Guide" as a general source for the DAO tooling landscape.
data.interpretation: Used to establish scale and stakes before walking through specific tool categories — the implicit argument is that this much real money being coordinated justifies investing in good tooling.
data.uncertainty: No specific dataset, date-stamp, or direct citation is attached to this exact figure within the article body; treat as an approximate, unverified-in-this-source aggregate statistic pending cross-check against a dedicated DAO analytics source (e.g. DeepDAO).

data.title: Decentralization
data.short_description: Spreading control and decision-making across many people instead of concentrating it in one place, so no single person, company, or office can shut things down, change the rules alone, or lock everyone else out. Framed in the article as a way of organizing power, not primarily a technology.
source_traditions: cooperatives
mutual aid networks
seed-saving circles / community seed swaps
rotating savings groups
crypto / DAO governance
data.toolkit_usage: Used as a foundations-layer explainer for community organizers and permaculturists new to crypto — reframes "decentralization" away from crypto-hype jargon toward practices (seed swaps, shared tooling, group decision-making) the audience already runs, then bridges to crypto-native tools (Snapshot, quadratic voting) and ReFi DAO's Local Nodes model as concrete implementations.
adjacent_meanings: technical/architectural decentralization (e.g. node distribution, consensus)
governance decentralization (who decides, per this article's framing)
economic decentralization (distributed ownership of value/tokens)
important_distinctions: decentralization-is-a-spectrum-not-a-switch — most real systems are hybrids (e.g. an open, tamper-proof ledger paired with founder-driven day-to-day decisions); the honest question is "who holds power, over what, and could they abuse it?" not a binary yes/no.

transparency-is-not-optional — the article argues real decentralization comes with *more* transparency, not less, and treats "no one's in charge" framing without visible decisions/money/people as a scam signal.
tensions: openness-vs-founder-control — a project can have a fully open, immutable public ledger while day-to-day decisions still run through a small founding group; the article treats this as normal-but-worth-naming rather than a failure state.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating decentralization as purely a technical/architecture property (node count, consensus mechanism) erases the article's core claim that it is fundamentally about organizing power and accountability — a community garden with a rotating steering group can be meaningfully decentralized without touching a blockchain.

data.title: Infrastructure Follows Function
data.short_description: Before choosing a knowledge-management tool, ask what work this part of the commons needs to do (explain a concept, inventory resources, track decisions, publish a guide) and pick the substrate that fits that job — not the tool with the nicest landing page. Corollary: no single tool needs to do everything; a healthy commons is usually a hybrid.
source_traditions: Regen Knowledge Commons Toolkit, Layer 10 (Infrastructure & Substrate)
data.toolkit_usage: Used as the article's governing principle for its tool-by-job directory, and again for its public/internal/private visibility-tier mapping (each tier gets its own substrate rather than one tool for everything).
adjacent_meanings: the portability test — "would your knowledge survive the tool dying?" (plain-text/Git as the durable baseline, everything else as a publishing or collaboration layer on top)
important_distinctions: A tool can make a workflow easier, but it can also distort the commons around its own assumptions — infrastructure should serve the work, not the reverse.
data.risks_of_flattening: Picking a tool for its polish or landing page rather than the specific job (explaining, inventorying, tracking, publishing) it needs to do — the article names this as the most common way commons rot.

data.title: Purpose-People-Place-Process-Practice (5P gathering framework)
data.short_description: A five-element design framework for gatherings — a specific purpose, a deliberate guest list, a matched space, a designed process arc (opening/ body/closing), and post-gathering practice (follow-through) — treating every gathering as an intentional design challenge rather than a default meetup script.
source_traditions: Priya Parker, "The Art of Gathering" (Riverhead Books, 2018)
Adrienne Maree Brown, "Emergent Strategy" (AK Press, 2017)
Open Civics Framework
data.toolkit_usage: Applied to four local-node gathering formats (Onboarding, Governance, Trust-Building, Learning) as the structural template organizers are instructed to work through before hosting.
adjacent_meanings: World Café
Fishbowl
Open Space Technology
Liberating Structures (33 facilitation methods)
Circle Practice (talking-piece format)
important_distinctions: "Purpose is not topic" — the article is explicit that "to learn about Web3" is a topic, not a purpose; a purpose states what will be different afterward.
"Agreements are mutual, rules are imposed" — the article deliberately avoids "ground rules" language in the Opening step.
tensions: Small-group-first, curated-guest-list design guidance vs. open/ inclusive-by-default community norms.
data.risks_of_flattening: The article attributes Circle Practice's talking-piece format and the small-group-before-large-group decision pattern to "many African and Indigenous traditions" and "many East African communities" in passing, secondary-source, non-attributed-to-a-specific-community language. Treating that as settled ethnography rather than a broad-strokes, unverified attribution risks flattening living traditions into a facilitation technique. See accompanying public-use-boundary.

data.title: Portability (knowledge commons)
data.short_description: The property that knowledge can move between tools, people, and organizations without rotting on the way — i.e., without depending on one vendor's proprietary format to remain readable.
source_traditions: plain-text/local-first software advocacy
version-control (Git) culture
data.toolkit_usage: The article's recommended floor for the Regen Knowledge Commons Toolkit itself: canonical content in Markdown tracked in Git, with structural metadata (title, tags, audience, source lineage) kept in YAML frontmatter rather than an app's hidden database.
adjacent_meanings: federation
vendor-lock-in
important_distinctions: portability-vs-federation — portability is about YOUR commons moving freely; federation is about connecting to OTHER people's commons without merging
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "plain text" alone as sufficient for portability ignores that structure (frontmatter/metadata schema) must also travel with the content, or the exported files become an unstructured pile.

data.title: Federation (knowledge commons)
data.short_description: Separate groups sharing knowledge with each other without merging into one unified database, closed-source software, or surrendering control over sensitive information.
source_traditions: KOI (Knowledge Organization Infrastructure) — BlockScience, Metagov, RMIT
Fediverse / ActivityPub (Mastodon)
data.toolkit_usage: Framed as mostly a governance-and-naming problem, not a tooling one: name what's public/internal/private, give shared things stable names, and you can federate "by hand" (a synced public folder) long before adopting a protocol like KOI-net.
adjacent_meanings: reference-identifier-rid
portability
important_distinctions: federation-vs-consolidation — federation preserves each group's boundaries and control; consolidation forces everyone into one shared database
identity-portability-vs-content-portability — ActivityPub/Mastodon already federates account identity/followers; it does not yet (as of 2025) federate the underlying post content
tensions: protocol-adoption-cost-vs-informal-federation — KOI-net gives structured sensor/processor/coordinator roles but requires real setup; an agreed shared folder of public Markdown is nearly free but has no formal guarantees
data.risks_of_flattening: Equating "federation" with any protocol adoption misses that the article's core claim is federation is achievable informally through named boundaries and stable references, without any protocol at all.

data.title: RID (Reference Identifier)
data.short_description: A stable label that points to a knowledge object (doc, message, record) without handing over the object itself — like a library call number.
source_traditions: KOI-net protocol (BlockScience, with Metagov and RMIT)
data.toolkit_usage: The mechanism cited as enabling federation without consolidation: organizations share the RID (the label/pointer) while keeping the underlying content and access rules under their own control. Attributed to BlockScience's Michael Zargham and Ilan Ben-Meir: "a stable concept of a reference as something distinct from (but referring to) an underlying referent is thus the mechanism that enables organizations to interoperate while retaining (and securing) their respective boundaries."
adjacent_meanings: federation
koi-net
important_distinctions: reference-vs-referent — the RID is the pointer/label; the referent (the actual document/message/record) is never itself transferred
data.risks_of_flattening: Only quoting the RID concept without KOI-net's supporting node roles (sensor/processor/coordinator) can make it sound like a naming scheme alone accomplishes federation; the roles are what actually move and transform the referenced knowledge across a network.

data.title: Crypto Wallet (keys, not money)
data.short_description: A crypto wallet does not store cryptocurrency itself — funds live on the blockchain. A wallet holds the cryptographic keys (a public key/address to receive with, and a private key that must never be shared) that prove a slice of the shared ledger belongs to you.
source_traditions: public-key cryptography
blockchain / distributed ledgers
data.toolkit_usage: Foundations-layer explainer for community organizers and permaculturists new to Web3; builds the public/private key distinction, then the recovery-phrase concept, then newer passkey-based "smart wallet" recovery, then hot-vs-cold wallet trade-offs, then names common scam patterns.
adjacent_meanings: traditional bank account (explicitly contrasted: no 'forgot password' or fraud department for a crypto wallet)
smart wallet (passkey + guardian-based recovery, positioned as a newer alternative to the classic recovery-phrase model)
important_distinctions: public-key-vs-private-key — the article's central operational distinction: the public key/address is safe to share (like a street address), the private key must never be shared (like the only key to your front door).

recovery-phrase-vs-smart-wallet-recovery — classic 12–24-word seed phrase backup vs. newer passkey + guardian-based recovery (e.g. Argent "Ready", Base App) that removes the single-written-artifact failure mode.
hot-wallet-vs-cold-wallet — always-online convenience (phone/browser) vs. offline hardware-device security; framed as a convenience/security trade-off, not a strict better/worse.
tensions: convenience-vs-security — the article's own suggested pattern is a small amount in a hot wallet for everyday use and larger amounts in cold storage, rather than resolving the trade-off one way.
data.risks_of_flattening: Treating "wallet" as synonymous with "exchange account" erases the article's core point that a wallet holds keys to a decentralized public ledger, not custodied funds — the whole recovery-phrase/scam-risk section only makes sense once that distinction is clear.

data.title: Regenerative Finance (ReFi)
data.short_description: Money flows that "build soil instead of mining it" — the article's core framing: rather than being extractive (treating a forest as worth more cut down than alive) or merely sustainable (doing less harm), ReFi aims to leave the system measurably healthier than it found it, using blockchain as a shared, tamper-resistant public record.
source_traditions: regenerative agriculture
blockchain / public ledgers
quadratic funding / mechanism design
carbon-market tokenization
