data.title: Governance Mechanism Design
data.summary: A framework for designing DAO/community governance mechanisms: six core mechanisms (token-weighted voting, one-person-one-vote, quadratic voting, conviction voting, consent-based decision making, futarchy) each with a best-fit context and named risks; a decision-type-to-mechanism mapping table; five design principles (match mechanism to context, minimize complexity, build in safeguards, iterate, transparency); and anti-manipulation measures against Sybil attacks, whale dominance, and collusion. Recommends starting with consent-based decisions for small groups and adding quadratic voting plus delegation as the group grows.
data.audience: DAO/community governance designers

data.title: Choosing a Model for Your Local Node
data.summary: Compares four organizational models local ReFi nodes actually use — the Collective (5-10 people, consensus), Working Groups (10-30, domain autonomy, ReFi DAO's "Network Initiatives" as the network-scale example), the Council (20-50+, consent-based governance, ReFi DAO's Steward Council as the example), and the Cooperative (15+, formal legal entity) — with a size/formality/decision-speed/legal-protection comparison table and guidance to evolve on purpose between models as group size and treasury size grow, rather than in crisis.

data.title: Funding Your Gatherings
data.summary: A four-tier framework for funding local-node gatherings, from zero-budget (shared meals, free venues, skill contributions) through low ($10-100: member contributions, passing the hat, monthly dues), medium ($100-500: local business sponsorship, small grants, web3-native funding via Gitcoin Grants/Giveth/Endaoment) to large ($500+: ticket sales, tiered sponsors, speaker budgets, ecosystem grants like the Ethereum Foundation ESP). Core argument: start with the cheapest thing that works, be transparent about money, and don't outspend your community's actual capacity.
data.audience: local regen node organizers planning their first gatherings
known_tensions: Recommends collecting contributions on-chain (multisig, Juicebox) as "the easiest real introduction to wallets your members will ever get" — a genuine convenience argument that also nudges a low-stakes social event toward on-chain tooling before it's strictly needed.

data.title: 1Hive
data.notes: Community building open governance tools; cited in the article as the source of the "free, fair, open, and humane" decentralization checklist used to structure the piece's "What Good Decentralization Looks Like" section.

data.title: Snapshot (snapshot.org)
data.notes: Gasless DAO voting tool described in the article as, as of early 2026, the most widely used voting tool in the space; votes are signed from each member's wallet and stored publicly. Article's "Go deeper" exercise points readers to browse a live DAO's votes there.

data.title: Obsidian
data.notes: Keeps everything as Markdown files in a folder ("vault") you fully control, with a graph view, backlinks, and a large plugin ecosystem. Named as the fit for "notes and thinking that a few people maintain" — because the files are plain Markdown on disk, the whole vault can be handed to the next maintainer with zero migration. Paid add-on: Obsidian Publish ($10/site/month, or $8/month billed annually).

data.title: Quartz
data.notes: Publishes an Obsidian vault straight to the web for free, with client-side full-text search and a graph view. Named as the most common free alternative to the paid Obsidian Publish add-on, and the shortest path from private notes to a public garden for teams already living in Obsidian.

data.title: Astro Starlight
data.notes: Heavier-duty documentation-site framework: sidebar navigation generated from file structure, dark mode, and built-in full-text search powered by Pagefind that runs entirely at build time (no external service, no API key, no monthly fee). The article notes the Regen Toolkit's own site runs on Starlight — named as the pick when a public commons needs to look and behave like proper docs.

data.title: BookStack
data.notes: Free, MIT-licensed, self-hosted wiki organizing content into a shelves -> books -> chapters -> pages hierarchy. Runs on ordinary PHP/MySQL hosting; named as the good default for a team knowledge base when you want order without much fiddling.

data.title: Outline
data.notes: The most polished self-hosted knowledge-base option — feels like a private Notion, with slash commands, nested docs, and real-time editing. Trade-off named in the article: no built-in username/password login, so it must be wired to an identity provider (Google, Slack, or any OIDC source) before anyone can sign in.

data.title: Wiki.js
data.notes: A Node.js wiki that can sync its content to a Git repository, giving a wiki UI and a plain-text-in-Git backup in one move. Named as the fit for technical teams that want non-technical people to edit comfortably while engineers keep a versioned copy.

data.title: GitBook
data.notes: Hosted docs platform with GitHub/GitLab sync; has a free tier and is free for open-source and nonprofit projects, but custom domains and team collaborators require a paid plan. Named as fine for a polished public handbook — the article's caution is to check the paywall boundary before depending on a feature that lives behind it.

data.title: Notion
data.notes: Polished block-based workspace, genuinely good for collaboration, but cited as a portability cautionary example: its export is lossy — databases come out as flat CSV snapshots that drop every view, filter, relation, and rollup; callouts export as raw HTML; nested pages produce filenames stuffed with 32-character IDs. After a few years, leaving Notion means manually reconstructing anything more complex than a plain page.

data.title: Logseq
data.notes: Open-source, local-first notes tool long loved for keeping notes as local Markdown. Cited as a portability caution: it shipped a new SQLite-backed "DB version" in 2025-2026 to fix performance limits on large graphs — faster, but data now lives in a database schema rather than portable text, and the two formats are not interoperable. The article's lesson: "file-on-disk" is a property to keep checking for, not assume, even for historically file-based tools.

data.title: GravityDAO
data.notes: A conflict-management and trust-building collective that grew out of the Token Engineering Commons to offer dispute resolution for Web3 projects. Cited in the article's closing section as a reminder that a commons's durability rests on coordination and care as much as on tool substrate — "tools preserve knowledge; they do not preserve trust."

data.title: The Art of Gathering
data.notes: "The Art of Gathering: How We Meet and Why It Matters" (Riverhead Books, 2018) — the primary source cited for the 5P gathering framework's core thesis that intentional structure, not a default script, is what makes gatherings work.

data.title: Liberating Structures
data.notes: A collection of 33 facilitation methods, each 10-30 minutes, designed to include everyone and release collective intelligence, replacing traditional presentations or managed discussions. Named as one of the Process-step formats that work well for local-node gatherings.

data.title: Obsidian
data.notes: Local-first notes app whose entire database is plain Markdown files on the user's own machine — used in the article as the concrete, non-technical-friendly proof that Markdown+Git portability works ("if Obsidian disappeared tomorrow, your vault would still open in TextEdit").

data.title: Giveth
data.notes: Donation platform running since 2016; lets anyone create a project page and receive donations directly with no platform fees taken out. Article uses it as the practical reason a community organizer would need a wallet at all.

data.title: MetaMask
data.notes: Named in the article as a common, free-to-install hot wallet (alongside Base App and Rainbow); the article's hands-on "Go deeper" exercise walks a reader through creating a wallet in MetaMask or the Base App.

data.title: Smart wallets with passkey/guardian recovery (Base App, Argent "Ready")
data.notes: Newer wallet category described in the article: replaces the lone written recovery phrase with passkey sign-in (Face ID/fingerprint) plus recovery via phone backup or trusted "guardians" who can help restore access but cannot spend funds. Named examples: the Base App (Coinbase's wallet, replaced the older Coinbase Wallet in 2025) and Argent (rebranded "Ready" in mid-2025). Grouped as one resource entry since the article treats them as one emerging pattern rather than profiling each separately; no single canonical URL given for the pattern itself.

data.title: Hardware / cold wallets (Ledger, Trezor)
data.notes: Small offline devices (about the size of a USB stick) that hold keys off the internet and only approve a payment when physically confirmed on the device; article's example of cold storage for larger holdings. Grouped as one entry (named examples Ledger and Trezor) rather than two, since the article treats them as one category with no distinguishing detail between the two brands.

data.title: Toucan Protocol
data.notes: Infrastructure that turns verified carbon credits into digital tokens; per the article, accounts for roughly 85% of digital carbon-credit volume and has supported ~$4B in trading volume, working alongside Gold Standard and Puro.earth. Involved in a 2023 Verra policy dispute over tokenizing already-retired credits (see linked claim-evidence).

data.title: Gitcoin (Quadratic Funding)
data.notes: Has run quadratic funding (a matching model where number of contributors matters more than size of any single donation) for years, per the article distributing over $60 million to more than 3,700 projects, and has since broadened into a mix of funding mechanisms.

data.title: Silvi
data.notes: Tree-stewardship platform where planters log each tree with GPS coordinates and a photo, making the claim independently checkable rather than taken on trust. Per the article, as of 2026 in open beta with 500+ planters across dozens of countries.

data.title: Grants Stack
data.notes: Gitcoin's open tooling for running a QF round end to end (create a program, choose Quadratic Funding, set round basics, payout token and matching pool, optional matching cap/minimum donation/Human Passport requirement, eligibility rules, then launch on-chain). The article frames the hard part as everything around the software — raising a real matching pool, recruiting genuine projects, and driving real donor turnout in a short window.

data.title: Maya Protocol
data.notes: Cross-chain liquidity protocol, per the article handling approximately $748 million in yearly volume and earning about $3 million in fees; cited as an example of a protocol transitioning to full DAO governance, where token holders will govern protocol upgrades and treasury allocations. No URL captured in the source article.

data.title: Aave (lending protocol)
data.notes: Cited twice in treasury-management.md — as a DeFi lending market where stablecoin holdings can be lent for yield, and as the example of a "reserve factor" mechanism where a portion of borrower interest flows directly to a protocol's ecosystem treasury as stablecoins (no token sales required). Also cited as a protocol DAOs can deposit native tokens into to borrow stablecoins without selling.

data.title: Gnosis Auction
data.notes: Cited in treasury-management.md as an example of a "batch auction" — aggregates buyer interest and sets a single clearing price, preventing manipulation, as one of the strategic token-sale approaches for diversifying a treasury with reduced market impact. No URL captured in the source article.

data.title: Octant
data.notes: "Evergreen" / yield-based funding mechanism cited as the article's example of the most structurally sustainable funding pattern: stakes 100,000 ETH and directs the bulk of each epoch's staking yield to public goods (over 2,340 ETH to 80+ projects across its first eight epochs; ninth epoch, the "Ethereum Stories" cohort, as of early 2026). Relevant to nodes able to build even a small endowment.

data.title: SKOS — Simple Knowledge Organization System (W3C)
data.notes: W3C standard (published 18 August 2009) for representing taxonomies, thesauri, and controlled vocabularies as linked data — prefLabel, altLabel, broader, narrower, related. Cited in ontology-vs-taxonomy.md as the recommended bridge: build a taxonomy in SKOS now, keep the door open to RDF/RDFS/OWL ontology work later without redoing it.

data.title: Protégé (Stanford ontology editor)
data.notes: Free, open-source OWL 2 ontology editor from Stanford, ships with reasoners like HermiT. Recommended in ontology-vs-taxonomy.md's "Stretch" exercise: model one real relationship (e.g. "Grant requires Report") and run the reasoner against three real records to test whether an ontology earns its keep before committing to building one.

data.title: Snapshot
data.notes: Gasless, signature-based off-chain voting used by tens of thousands of communities. Named in the article's complexity-trigger table as the boring, durable 2026 default for a small node that starts voting often and wants it free and verifiable — explicitly contrasted with the older DAOstack/Alchemy stack, called out as stale advice.

data.title: Safe (Wallet)
data.notes: Multisig smart-contract wallet (formerly Gnosis Safe), named in the article's complexity-trigger table as the default treasury tool once real money is pooled and one person shouldn't hold the keys alone (e.g. 3-of-5 signatures); deploys on Base or Arbitrum for under a dollar.

data.title: hOurworld
data.notes: Free timebanking software that runs hundreds of active timebanks across dozens of countries, no blockchain required. Named in the article as one valid "way to track value" for a minimum viable node — the rule given is to pick the simplest tool everyone already trusts, offline or on-chain.

data.title: Obsidian (local-first note tool)
data.notes: Local-first note tool cited in source-systems.md as an example of stewardship + ongoing additions in plain files you own — stores notes as plain Markdown with bidirectional linking so the knowledge graph builds itself as you write. Recommended in the "Stretch" exercise for standing up a real source system.

data.title: Logseq (local-first note tool)
data.notes: Local-first, Markdown-based note tool with bidirectional linking, cited in source-systems.md alongside Obsidian as a tool that gives stewardship and ongoing additions in plain files you own.

data.title: Citation File Format (CITATION.cff)
data.notes: Plain-text file dropped in a GitHub repo root; on the default branch GitHub auto-generates a "Cite this repository" link with APA/BibTeX citations. Cited in source-systems.md as a concrete, machine-readable answer to "who made this and how do I credit them," and recommended in the "Go deeper" exercise.

data.title: Ethereum Attestation Service (EAS)
data.notes: Open standard for recording signed, tamper-evident attestations (on-chain or off-chain, free schemas); article states over 9.5 million attestations recorded as of mid-2026. Positioned as the recommended plumbing for a local node to attest workshops, plantings, or shipped deliverables. Explorer: easscan.org.

data.title: Hypercerts Protocol
data.notes: Verifiable records of a piece of impactful work, used so funders can allocate capital against proven contributions rather than pitches; per the article, used in Gitcoin Grants 24 (GG24) as peer-reviewed hypercerts, and shifted in 2026 from ERC-1155 tokens on Optimism toward living digital records built on the AT Protocol.

data.title: Regen Network Registry
data.notes: Issues ecological credits against published MRV methodologies; article recommends routing verified ecological outcomes through this registry once a node is doing ecological work, ahead of reaching for heavier dMRV (satellite/sensor-based digital MRV) tooling.

data.title: The Giving Block
data.notes: Platform that lets nonprofits accept crypto donations ("as easy as adding a donate button" per the article) and publishes an annual crypto-giving report cited for the 386% YoY donation growth figure and the 70%-of- Forbes-Top-100-charities figure.

data.title: Grassroots Economics / Sarafu Network
data.notes: Runs the Sarafu Network in Kenya — local "community asset vouchers" for trading goods/services when national-currency cash is scarce, now on the Celo blockchain, with feature-phone (USSD) access requiring no smartphone or internet plan. Cited in what-is-blockchain.md as a live community-currency network, with usage figures captured separately as a claim-evidence object (see 08-claim-evidence.yaml).

data.title: Regen Network
data.notes: Blockchain platform issuing science-backed ecological credits, per the article: pays land stewards for measurable ecological work (restored soil, biodiversity) by recording verified ecological data on-chain and issuing purchasable credits. Flagged high_risk because ecological/MRV (measurement, reporting, verification) claims are a standing high-risk trigger — the specific claim that "the regeneration actually happened" is captured separately with a public-use-boundary (see 09-claim-evidence.yaml / 10-public-use-boundary.yaml).

data.title: Walmart / Hyperledger Fabric mango traceability case study
data.notes: Enterprise-blockchain comparison in what-is-blockchain.md: Walmart traces leafy greens through Hyperledger Fabric (an enterprise blockchain framework stewarded by the Linux Foundation's Decentralized Trust group). The specific pilot result (mango origin traceback time) is captured separately as a claim-evidence object.

data.title: Bankless Academy: Blockchain Basics
data.notes: Free, open-source, interactive, no-wallet-required lesson recommended in the article's "Go deeper" exercise for readers new to crypto.

data.title: ReFi DAO Local Node Incubator / Regen Coordination Hub
data.notes: Published Local Node Toolkit and incubator program; runs registration through Luma and structures sessions around Liberating Structures facilitation formats. Cited as the main "don't build the stack alone" on-ramp for new local-node organizers, alongside Greenpill Network and the wider Regen Coordination constellation (BioFi, Bloom Network).

data.title: Glo Dollar (USDGLO)
data.notes: A fully-backed, audited stablecoin that donates 100% of the interest earned on its reserves to public goods and anti-poverty programs. Cited as ReFi Medellín's example of a treasury choice matching mission — but the article notes Medellín had a community and treasury before adopting it (tooling follows people, not the reverse).

data.title: MADR — Markdown Architectural Decision Records
data.notes: Widely used template for Architecture Decision Records with a built-in status field (proposed / accepted / deprecated / superseded). Cited in review-and-maturity.md as a working example of a granted-vs-self-claimed maturity ladder, and as a "Go deeper" recommendation for adopting a status field in page frontmatter.

data.title: Diátaxis (documentation framework)
data.notes: Daniele Procida's documentation framework, adopted by Gatsby and Cloudflare. Cited in review-and-maturity.md as useful for deciding what *kind* of page you are reviewing before rating its maturity.

data.title: M-Pesa
data.notes: East African mobile-money service used in the article as a real-world example of a system that "started with a relatively centralized model" — useful for rapid deployment but carrying single-infrastructure vulnerabilities.

data.title: Coinbase Wallet
data.notes: Ranked easiest for complete beginners; distributed via Google Play Store per the article, no direct URL given so link_status is unresolved.

data.title: MetaMask
data.notes: Described as the industry standard for Web3-app compatibility; supports many blockchains and has a desktop browser-extension option per the article; no direct URL given so link_status is unresolved.

data.title: Trust Wallet
data.notes: Supports 100+ blockchains per the article and is owned by Binance; built-in browser for Web3 apps; no direct URL given so link_status is unresolved.

data.title: Rainbow Wallet
data.notes: Praised for Ethereum and Base network support and polished design; fewer coins supported than the others per the article; no direct URL given so link_status is unresolved.

data.title: Ledger Academy - How Does a Blockchain Transaction Work
data.notes: Educational article cited as "[Source S]" for both of how-transactions-work.md's direct quotations on private-key signing authority and block-confirmation immutability.

data.title: Grassroots Economics: Sarafu Network
data.notes: A Kenya-based network letting people exchange Community Asset Vouchers (promises of future goods/labor/services) through shared "commitment pools" that track who has offered, taken, and fulfilled promises over time. Cited in the article as the clearest working example of trust backed by relationships rather than substituted by technology.

data.title: Safe (multisig wallets)
data.notes: Standard multisig wallet (formerly Gnosis Safe) for on-chain treasuries. Article recommends a 3-of-5 signer setup as a transparency practice: every member gets a public, real-time ledger of every movement, and no single person can move funds alone.

data.title: Human Passport
data.notes: Formerly Gitcoin Passport — a proof-of-personhood / sybil-resistance tool letting a node confirm members are unique real people, not one person wearing ten wallets. Article frames it as scaffolding toward human trust for larger, open networks, not a permanent replacement for it.

data.title: GreenPill Network
data.notes: A regen network of local chapters, named as a sister model to ReFi DAO's local nodes; flagged as a source-system candidate for a future register-source pass (it curates its own chapter directory).

data.title: Canòdrom (Barcelona's Ateneu d'Innovació Digital i Democràtica)
data.notes: Barcelona's public digital-innovation and democracy centre, mapped by ReFi Barcelona as an aligned local venue for hands-on workshops; a public civic venue, not a private location, so no high-risk trigger.

data.title: MetaMask
data.notes: Recommended free wallet for exploring Ethereum with test ETH on Sepolia testnet, no real money required.

data.title: Ethereum Name Service (ENS)
data.notes: Described in the article's "Try This" exercise as a phonebook for Ethereum addresses — search any ENS name with no account needed.

data.title: KoboToolbox
data.notes: Named in the article as one of the basic-smartphone-friendly dMRV data collection tools (alongside ODK and Google Forms). No URL given in this article's own text; not invented here.

data.title: Notion
data.notes: Recommended in the article as the "structured and powerful" documentation tier: built-in databases and templates, good for wikis and knowledge bases, works on mobile and desktop.

data.title: GitBook
data.notes: Recommended in the article as the "technical and durable" tier alongside GitHub: version control, markdown-based, built for long-term persistence; article specifically recommends it for communities that want documentation to survive platform changes.

data.title: Luma (lu.ma)
data.notes: Article's cited default for regen-scene event listing/registration. Free events have no platform fee; paid tickets carry a 5% platform fee plus Stripe processing (~2.9% + 30¢/ticket); "Luma Plus" removes the 5% fee for $69/month ($59/month billed annually). Pricing verified as of mid-2026 per the article; note prices shift, re-verify before relying on this.

data.title: Galxe OAT (On-chain Achievement Token)
data.notes: Article's cited active alternative to POAP for attendance/achievement badges as of March 2026 (POAP entered maintenance mode — see accompanying signal). Organizers design a badge campaign on galxe.com; attendees claim it for free (gasless) by email or QR code.

data.title: Greenpill Network
data.notes: Global regen network with 12 active local chapters as of mid-2026 (per article); also publishes a Local Regen Guide PDF (greenpill.network/pdf/local-regen-guide.pdf).

data.title: DeepDAO
data.notes: Cited in the article's references as the source for DAO statistics and landscape data (used to ground the "over 215 DAOs / $9.5B / ~500,000 active members" figure). Flagged as a possible source-system candidate (a living analytics database) but not built out into a full source-system card here — no steward/return_path detail is given in this article.

data.title: Tri-Ethnic Center Community Readiness Model (assessment manuals)
data.notes: The nine-stage Community Readiness Model and its assessment manuals, developed by the Tri-Ethnic Center for Prevention Research at Colorado State University, cited in is-community-ready.md as the framework underlying its launch-readiness guidance.

data.title: Sarafu (Grassroots Economics)
data.notes: Kenyan community currency run by nonprofit Grassroots Economics; USSD/basic-phone access, no smartphone or bank account required; reports 26,000+ people across ~290 communities (per article, as of source date).

data.title: Silvi Protocol
data.notes: Pays people to plant/steward trees; records GPS coordinates and photos per tree so claims can be independently checked rather than taken on faith (MRV-style verification pattern). This is an ecological/carbon-adjacent claim — see assessed-but-excluded note on the encyclopedia-entry object; not elevated to high_risk here since the article does not itself assert a specific carbon quantity, only the verification method.

data.title: Sarafu Network (Grassroots Economics)
data.notes: Kenyan community currency reported (as of early 2026, per article) to support roughly 26,000 people across ~290 communities, running on the low-energy Celo blockchain; same project already ingested from common-concerns.md as "Sarafu (Grassroots Economics)" — duplication across source articles is expected at ingest time and left for the review/dedupe layer.

data.title: Regen Network
data.notes: Lets land stewards register regenerative projects and issue ecological credits for measured outcomes (e.g. soil carbon), sold to buyers directly per the article; flagged as a source-system candidate for a future register-source pass since it's a living registry/marketplace.

data.title: Glo Dollar
data.notes: A nonprofit digital dollar whose cash/US-government-bond reserve interest is donated to charities the holder chooses; the article names GiveDirectly as a major recipient.

data.title: Axie Infinity
data.notes: Cited in the article's Gaming and Virtual Economies section as an example of NFT-based in-game asset ownership and play-to-earn mechanics.

data.title: IBM Food Trust
data.notes: Cited in the article's Supply Chains and Product Authenticity section as an example of blockchain-based produce/food traceability from farm to store — relevant to communities producing goods for export wanting to prove ethical or fair-price production.

data.title: Leadership on the Line (Heifetz & Linsky)
data.notes: Full citation: Heifetz, Ronald, and Marty Linsky. "Leadership on the Line: Staying Alive Through the Dangers of Leading." Harvard Business Review Press, 2002. Listed in the article's references alongside Stone & Patton's "Difficult Conversations" (Penguin, 2000), ICA:UK's "Facilitative Leadership" (ica-uk.co.uk), and Greenpill Local's "Distributed Leadership in Practice" (greenpill.live) — those three are noted here rather than split into separate objects (see assessed-but-excluded on the encyclopedia-entry candidate).

data.title: GitBook (change requests)
data.notes: Recommended as a pull-request-equivalent review container for non-technical reviewers: its "change request" workflow gives a visual review link so a program lead or legal reviewer can approve without touching Git.

data.title: Vale (prose linter)
data.notes: Open-source prose linter recommended as a GitHub Action: checks every pull request against style rules (banned hype words, heading conventions, terminology) and posts inline comments before a human reviews, so human review time goes to accuracy rather than nitpicks.

data.title: BIP39 Specification (Bitcoin Improvement Proposals)
data.notes: The original standard defining the 2,048-word list and how seed phrases are generated; cited in the article's References section.

data.title: Safe (safe.global)
data.notes: The widely used multisig smart wallet (e.g. 3-of-5 signer approval) recommended in the article as the group-treasury alternative to a single person holding one seed phrase.

data.title: MetaMask Support: Restoring and Understanding a Secret Recovery Phrase
data.notes: Combines the article's two cited MetaMask support links: the step-by-step restore guide and the plain explanation of why the phrase matters and how to keep it secure.

data.title: LocalCoinSwap
data.notes: Non-custodial peer-to-peer crypto marketplace operating in 190+ countries with roughly a 1% fee, named in how-to-get-crypto.md as a 2026-current working P2P option (superseding the now-defunct Paxful).

data.title: Bisq
data.notes: Open-source, non-custodial desktop peer-to-peer exchange with no sign-up and no company holding funds, named in how-to-get-crypto.md as the privacy-focused P2P option.

data.title: Safe
data.notes: Standard multisig wallet for shared, no-single-point-of-control community treasuries, per the article.

data.title: Open Collective
data.notes: Fiscal-hosting platform; budget becomes a public ledger anyone can audit in real time. Hosts like The Social Change Nest handle accounting/compliance.

data.title: Greenpill Network
data.notes: Runs Greenpill-specific quadratic funding rounds for local chapters during Gitcoin events, and mints hypercerts for each chapter; around a dozen active chapters worldwide per the article.

data.title: ReFi DAO
data.notes: Regen coordination network; home of the Local Node program and match-funding history (via Gitcoin and Giveth match pools) per the article.

data.title: Giveth
data.notes: Zero-fee crypto donation platform with a GIVbacks rewards program (GIV tokens to donors); used for match-funding pools per the article.

data.title: Hypercerts
data.notes: On-chain impact certificates for recording and retroactively funding regenerative work; minted by Greenpill for its chapters per the article.

data.title: Gitcoin Grants (tips for grant success)
data.notes: Source of the article's core proposal-writing advice: lead with a TL;DR including how you'll spend the money, list team qualifications, show you're iterating, and give supporters time to set up wallets.

data.title: POAP (Proof of Attendance Protocol)
data.notes: Cited in the article as a way to make a newcomer's first event a "small gift, not a test" — a free collectible NFT minted to attendees, issued on Gnosis Chain so both organizers and attendees pay nothing. Distributed via QR code at the event.

data.title: L2Beat
data.notes: Cited as a Layer 2 comparison and risk-assessment tool in the article's References.

data.title: Etherscan
data.notes: Named in "Try This" Exercise 1 as the place to look up a real deployed contract (e.g. Uniswap or OpenSea) and see its layout/functions.

data.title: MetaMask (test network)
data.notes: Named in "Try This" Exercise 3 as a browser wallet to switch to a test network and experiment with transactions using free fake currency, no real money required.

data.title: Chainlink: What Is a Blockchain Oracle?
data.notes: Cited in the article's References list for the oracle concept.

data.title: Argent
data.notes: Mobile-focused wallet with social recovery built in (a trusted guardian can help recover access instead of requiring a multisig threshold). Article frames social recovery and multisig as addressing different problems: simpler/more flexible for individual wallets, but multisig "remains the better choice" for community treasuries needing ongoing, legitimate multi-person access.

data.title: Gitcoin Grants
data.notes: Listed under "Funding Support" as an organization that funds community projects; no URL given in this article (see funding-gatherings.md and funding-your-node.md for fuller treatment with URLs).

data.title: Giveth
data.notes: Listed under "Funding Support" as an organization that funds community projects; no URL given in this article (see giveth-donations.md for full treatment with URLs and mechanics).

data.title: Snapshot (snapshot.org)
data.notes: Gasless DAO voting tool; article cites "over 7,500 groups now use it" (daotimes.com/snapshot-dao-tool-report-for-2025/) and recommends browsing real groups' live votes with no account or wallet as the "Start here" exercise.

data.title: Regen Network
data.notes: Cited as the article's example of "an on-chain registry for ecological credits" — verified outcomes (carbon stored, grassland restored) become "ecocredits" that buyers purchase and permanently retire, with proof recorded openly rather than in a private spreadsheet.

data.title: Gitcoin
data.notes: Cited as the article's example of "community-directed funding" via quadratic funding, a matching system where many small donations count for far more than a few large ones. Article states Gitcoin has channelled "over $67 million to more than 5,000 public-good projects" this way.

data.title: Mento (Celo local-currency stablecoins)
data.notes: Issues local-currency stablecoins on Celo (a mobile-first Ethereum Layer 2), including cKES (Kenya), cREAL (Brazil), cCOP (Colombia), and PUSO (Philippines) — cited as a "borrow rather than build" tool for community currency.

data.title: The Giving Block
data.notes: Described as one of the largest crypto-donation platforms, used by many major nonprofits, offering a suite of tools beyond just accepting donations. No URL given in source article; link_status left unresolved.

data.title: Infinite Giving
data.notes: Described as designed specifically for nonprofits, focused on ease of use, good for smaller orgs just starting out; also referenced (with sourced messaging quote) in the sibling communicating-stakeholders.md article. No URL given in this source article; link_status left unresolved.

data.title: ENS DAO
data.notes: Cited as the article's example of token-weighted voting, managing Ethereum Name Service decisions.

data.title: SafeDAO
data.notes: Cited as the article's example of multi-signature governance, coordinating treasury management and protocol upgrades.

data.title: Snapshot (gasless off-chain DAO voting)
data.notes: Supports yes/no, approval, quadratic, and ranked-choice voting per the article; its limitation is noted as double-voting risk since signatures aren't submitted directly to the blockchain.

data.title: Obsidian
data.notes: Free desktop app that edits a folder of local markdown files; gives wikilinks, backlinks, and a graph view with no account required. Paid Obsidian Publish ($8/mo annual, $10/mo month-to-month) turns a vault into a hosted site.

data.title: Quartz
data.notes: Free, open-source (MIT), currently v4, static-site generator built for Obsidian vaults — carries wikilinks, backlinks, graph, and full-text search to a published site. SuperBenefit ran Obsidian+Quartz before migrating to a custom Astro build.

data.title: GravityDAO
data.notes: Provides conflict management and trust-building for DAOs; cited in the article as an example of communities treating a commons' soft infrastructure (shared meaning, maintained agreements, surfaced tension) as active-care work, analogous to garden tending.

data.title: Gitcoin Passport
data.notes: Aggregates web3 activity/verifications ("stamps") into a score used by grants programs and DAOs to confirm a real, active participant rather than a bot/sybil; used to weight Gitcoin Grants quadratic-funding matching.

data.title: Disco.xyz
data.notes: Described as built specifically for managing and sharing web3 identity and credentials in readable form ("a CV layer on top of your wallet"); no URL given in source, link_status left unresolved pending verification.

data.title: Every.org (crypto donations)
data.notes: The article's explicit "start here" recommendation — free, ~15 minutes to set up, converts crypto donations to fiat automatically. Best for organizations starting out or with smaller operations.

data.title: Silvi
data.notes: Named as a program using dMRV to prove tree planting and pay for impact. No URL given in the article itself; link_status set to "unresolved" pending a human confirming the canonical Silvi Protocol URL (a "silvi-protocol.md" article exists elsewhere in this site's open work orders and may cover it in more depth).

data.title: DefiLlama Stablecoins Dashboard
data.notes: Recommended in "Try This: Start here" as a live, no-money-required way to see stablecoin sizes and peg stability; flagged is_source_system_candidate since it is a continuously updated living data source, not a static document.

data.title: Glo Dollar (USDGLO)
data.notes: A fiat-backed stablecoin that donates 100% of reserve profit to public goods and anti-poverty charities (default recipient GiveDirectly per the article); named as a concrete ReFi-aligned stablecoin example.

data.title: Wyoming DUNA
data.notes: Decentralized Unincorporated Nonprofit Association, effective July 1, 2024 — DAO-specific legal wrapper requiring 100+ members and meaningful on-chain governance; Uniswap Foundation's DUNI (est. via governance vote, 2025) is named as a worked adopter example. Not a substitute for legal counsel; see paired public-use-boundary object.

data.title: Etherscan
data.notes: Public block explorer recommended in the "Try This" exercise to see how little privacy a public chain actually offers — any wallet or transaction can be looked up.

data.title: Bankless Academy — Foundations of Decentralization
data.notes: Listed in the article's References as a source for its foundations-of- decentralization framing; link_status set to unresolved since the exact course URL/page was not independently verified for this ingestion.

data.title: Gitcoin
data.notes: Named as one of the tools (funding) the illustrative "ReFi Africa" group used to build its community from scratch.

data.title: Snapshot
data.notes: Named as one of the tools (decisions/voting) the illustrative "ReFi Africa" group used for governance.

data.title: Bankless Academy
data.notes: Cited as the source the whole guide draws from ("This guide draws from Bankless Academy's educational resources") and as the learn-to-earn platform giving collectible badges for completed lessons; no URL given in the source article, link_status left unresolved pending verification.

data.title: Loomio
data.notes: Named in is-dao-right.md's "A Note on Alternatives" as a simple voting tool suitable for low-tech communities choosing a lighter-weight decision process instead of a DAO.

data.title: Arbitrum
data.notes: Named as an example Layer 2 network for cheap, fast transactions; no URL given in this article.

data.title: Optimism
data.notes: Named as an example Layer 2 network for cheap, fast transactions; no URL given in this article.

data.title: Otter.ai
data.notes: Meeting transcription tool, named as the default place a small team should start. Free tier: 300 transcription minutes/month, capped at 30 minutes per conversation, with automated summaries and action items. Pro plan ($8.33/month billed annually) lifts to 1,200 minutes. Article warns transcription pricing changes often and to verify current limits before committing.

data.title: Google NotebookLM
data.notes: Free with a Google account; load up to 50 sources on the free tier and ask questions grounded in exactly those documents, with citations to the passage. Article's recommended "find answers" leg of a starter stack: load governance docs, past meeting summaries, and the founding agreement.

data.title: Smart Connections (Obsidian plugin)
data.notes: Obsidian plugin that builds embeddings entirely on-device, enabling semantic search and chat with a vault fully offline, with nothing sent to the cloud. Article's recommended tool for teams whose commons holds sensitive community data or that want the archive to outlive any one company.

data.title: Dune Analytics
data.notes: On-chain analytics platform cited as the tool that enables the transparency described in the article (detecting suspicious token movements etc.); flagged as a source-system candidate since it's a living, queryable data environment, not a static reference.

data.title: GitHub CODEOWNERS
data.notes: Described as turning the Editor role into a merge rule: a CODEOWNERS file auto-requests the right reviewer when someone opens a PR touching their owned paths.

data.title: all-contributors
data.notes: A bot + specification for recognizing non-code contributions (docs, review, mentoring, event organizing) via a comment command that updates the repo README's contributor list.

data.title: Gravity DAO
data.notes: A conflict-management collective from the Token Engineering Commons, cited as the model for the Facilitator role — treats disagreement as "transformational opportunities" toward good-faith compromise.

data.title: Protocol Guild
data.notes: Onchain registry funding 180+ Ethereum core maintainers across 29 teams, cited as an example of keeping funding strictly separate from protocol decision power (so getting paid never buys a vote).

data.title: Wikimedia Stewards
data.notes: Globally elected Wikimedia role, deliberately barred from using its powers on wikis where the steward is an active local editor — cited as a real-world example of keeping stewardship about the commons rather than home-turf power.

data.title: Greenpill Network
data.notes: Runs local chapters and the Greenpill podcast (hosted by Kevin Owocki, Gitcoin co-founder); article names roughly a dozen active chapters as of mid-2026 including Cape Town, Nairobi, Taipei, Rio de Janeiro, NYC, and London Ontario.

data.title: Safe (formerly Gnosis Safe)
data.notes: Cited in the article as "the most widely adopted multi-sig wallet for DAOs and organizations," offering role-based access control, transaction limits/spending caps, time-locks on large transactions, and audit trails. Same tool also cited in the sibling recovery-planning.md article in this batch.

data.title: Ithaca Hours
data.notes: Longest-running time-based community currency (New York, USA; launched 1991). One Ithaca Hour equals one hour of labour — cited as the canonical time-based-unit example.

data.title: Brixton Pound
data.notes: Local paper currency for Brixton, London, UK, with some later blockchain adoption — cited as a value-based-unit example distinct from the time-based Ithaca Hours.

data.title: Klima DAO
data.notes: Bridges verified off-chain carbon credits onto the blockchain for trading; no URL given in the source article's References list.

data.title: Base (Layer 2 network)
data.notes: Optimistic Rollup built by Coinbase; launched 2023 and described in the article as one of the friendliest L2 options for newcomers, compatible with MetaMask/Uniswap and most existing Ethereum tools.

data.title: Arbitrum
data.notes: Optimistic Rollup, one of the article's two named "main examples" of Optimistic Rollups (with Base); also named as an ecosystem that funds public goods via grants/retroactive funding.

data.title: L2BEAT
data.notes: Independent site tracking Layer 2 stats and risk assessments, cited in the article's references for doing due diligence on newer/less established L2 networks. Flagged is_source_system_candidate: true — it is a maintained, living data resource, not a static link; a future ingest pass could register it as a full source-system card.

data.title: MetaMask
data.notes: Named in the article as a well-known non-custodial wallet; described as generating the seed phrase on-device and signing transactions locally without exposing the private key to the internet.

data.title: Ledger (hardware wallet)
data.notes: Named alongside Trezor as a hardware wallet offering an additional security layer by storing private keys offline; article recommends this for holding significant value.

data.title: Snapshot
related_concepts: DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization) vs. Local Node
data.notes: Free, gasless, off-chain voting platform; article states 35,000+ communities use it, with a November 2025 "Spaces 2.0" release adding custom domains (e.g. vote.yournode.eth). For onchain/binding votes, the article points to Snapshot X (Starknet) as the live path after Tally's March 2026 wind-down — see the paired claim-evidence object.

data.title: Hats Protocol
related_concepts: DAO (Decentralized Autonomous Organization) vs. Local Node
data.notes: Turns each responsibility (treasury signer, onboarding lead, events coordinator) into an onchain "hat" (ERC-1155 token) so permissions follow the role rather than the person; article states it is trusted by 50+ DAOs. Recommended only once "who is allowed to do what" is a real source of confusion, not pre-emptively.

data.title: Cryptosteel (metal seed-phrase storage)
data.notes: A metal seed-phrase storage product mentioned in hot-vs-cold.md as protection for a wallet's recovery seed phrase against fire and water damage, as an alternative/complement to paper backups.

data.title: Cryptocurrency Security Standards (CCSS)
data.notes: Referenced in hot-vs-cold.md's References as a place for deeper security practices beyond the article's introductory hot/cold framing.

data.title: Read the Docs — deprecating content guide
data.notes: Documentation-hosting platform's guide recommending a warning banner atop a stale page rather than pulling it — deleting "will break existing links, and you don't necessary [sic] want to make the content inaccessible" — and, when a page must be removed, creating redirects to replacement content rather than letting links break.

data.title: Grafana Writers' Toolkit — deprecate or remove content
data.notes: Draws a sharp line: deprecated means "planned for removal in a future release," removed means "removed and no longer supported." Grafana notifies users two minor releases in advance before anything disappears, with a stock notice template ("Starting with [release], [feature] is deprecated. It will be removed in a future release.").

data.title: Quartz
data.notes: Open-source static-site generator that turns an Obsidian or Markdown folder into a published site. Article notes it lets teams carry a publish/maturity flag in each note's frontmatter, so the growth state that helps the writer also signals trust to readers.

data.title: Mondragon Worker Cooperative Federation
data.notes: Basque Country worker-cooperative federation spanning manufacturing, retail, finance, and education; cited as the best-known large worker-cooperative example, sustaining employment through economic cycles.

data.title: GravityDAO
data.notes: Cited as the governance-half example: brings conflict management and trust creation to DAOs via alternative dispute resolution rather than top-down arbitration. Used in the article to make the point that a commons' hardest maintenance problems are usually disagreements about what's true/settled, not technical ones.

data.title: OpenZeppelin
data.notes: Cited in the article's References as the widely used open-source implementation library for ERC token standards.

data.title: OpenSea
data.notes: Named in "Try This" Exercise 3 as a marketplace to browse "Collections" and see how ERC-721 NFTs and ERC-1155 multi-token assets are presented.

data.title: Dublin Core
data.notes: Fifteen broad, generic metadata properties (Title, Creator, Date, Subject, Description, Type, Source, Rights, and seven more) standardized internationally as ISO 15836, maintained since the 1990s. Article recommends borrowing its battle-tested field names (e.g. Creator, Subject) rather than inventing new ones.

data.title: Murmurations Protocol
data.notes: A regen-adjacent network protocol maintaining a public field library of pre-defined, reusable metadata fields (e.g. `longitude`, not `long`). Cited as the example of why shared field names matter across a network of communities — directly analogous to this toolkit's own federation concerns. Flagged is_source_system_candidate: true — a future ingest pass could register Murmurations as a full source-system peer (it maintains a living, updatable field library, not a static document).

data.title: remark-lint-frontmatter-schema
data.notes: Validates markdown frontmatter against a JSON Schema (types, required fields, enums), with inline VS Code warnings and auto-fix suggestions — recommended for plain-markdown repositories that are not using an Astro/Zod content-collection setup.

data.title: SuperBenefit Knowledge Garden — Anticapture Framework
data.notes: A governance framework focused on resisting concentration of power (distributing authority rather than replacing one central power with another); flagged as a source-system candidate because it's a living knowledge garden, not a static document — a future ingestion pass should register it properly via skills/register-source with a return_path.

data.title: Solana
data.notes: High-throughput (tens of thousands TPS), sub-cent-fee chain using Proof of History to parallelize transaction processing. Article flags network outage history and non-EVM tooling/skills as tradeoffs. Suited, per the article, to high-frequency low-value transactions: community token distributions, micro-donations, at-scale carbon-credit tracking.

data.title: Cosmos
data.notes: Lets a project launch its own purpose-built blockchain (via the Cosmos SDK and Tendermint consensus) that stays interoperable with other chains via the Inter-Blockchain Communication (IBC) protocol. Article frames this as suited to projects needing full control over their own economics (e.g. a regional community currency with tailored governance) but flags running your own chain — validators, community participation, maintenance — as a major commitment, "probably overkill" for most regenerative communities.

data.title: Polkadot
data.notes: A central relay chain provides shared security to connected specialized chains ("parachains") that lease a parachain slot rather than running their own validator network. Article frames this as appealing for a regenerative project that needs reliable infrastructure without a large team.

data.title: Avalanche
data.notes: Uses a consensus mechanism distinct from Proof of Work and standard Proof of Stake to process thousands of transactions per second while maintaining decentralization; its subnet architecture lets a project spin up an independent blockchain network with its own tokens, rules, and validator set within the Avalanche ecosystem. Article suggests subnets fit a carbon-tracking network, community currency, or local regenerative economy that wants its own chain while staying connected to a larger ecosystem.

data.title: Near Protocol
data.notes: Prioritizes developer experience and user accessibility; uses "Nightshade" sharding to process blockchain data in parallel pieces, and leans on account abstraction to make wallet experiences feel more familiar to non-crypto-native users. Article notes Near has funded carbon removal for its own operations and frames its usability focus as aligned with bringing web3 to people outside the space already.

data.title: Centrifuge (RWA tokenization platform)
data.notes: Named in the article as a company/platform for tokenizing assets (issuer/platform category); article gives no URL, so link_status is unresolved rather than invented.

data.title: Polymath (RWA tokenization platform)
data.notes: Named alongside Centrifuge as an example platform to explore tokenized assets; article gives no URL, so link_status is unresolved rather than invented.

data.title: BERTopic
data.notes: MIT-licensed Python library (Maarten Grootendorst) for embedding-based topic discovery: turns documents into embeddings, clusters them, and labels each cluster with its most distinctive words. Supports guided topic modeling via a seed_topic_list. Article's recommended tool for a one-time "discovery" pass to design a taxonomy, not a daily driver.

data.title: Auto Classifier (Obsidian plugin)
data.notes: Obsidian plugin (by HyeonseoNam) that classifies notes against three reference modes: all tags in the vault, a filtered regex subset, or a manual hand-curated category list (the supervised "bucketing" pattern, built in). Works with any OpenAI-compatible API (OpenAI, local Ollama, LocalAI) and can also use the Jina AI Classifier, which has a free tier.

data.title: AI Tagger (obsidian-ai-tagger)
data.notes: Obsidian plugin for one-click and batch tagging across many LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Groq, Mistral, local Ollama). Returns up to five tags you've used before and at most three genuinely new ones per note, so existing vocabulary is reused first and novelty is rationed — the article holds this up as a model for a deliberate "new tag" escape hatch reviewed in weekly batches.

data.title: Ollama
data.notes: Runs open LLMs locally. Article frames running classification through Ollama as more than a cost choice: it keeps unreviewed community material on the team's own machine instead of shipping it to a third-party API — the same public/private boundary the Toolkit's infrastructure layer asks teams to respect for high-risk or sensitive material.

data.title: Snapshot (gasless DAO voting)
data.notes: Described as the most widely used DAO voting tool, with tens of thousands of community spaces per the article; keeps votes off-chain and gasless via wallet-signature verification.

data.title: Aragon
data.notes: A no-code platform for creating a DAO, issuing voting rights, and setting rules across several blockchains, per the article.

data.title: ReFi DAO Local Nodes
data.notes: Connects regenerative-finance projects worldwide through self-governing Local Nodes per the article; same organization already registered as a source-system from types-of-gatherings.md ingestion — flagged here again as a candidate since duplication across source articles is expected and left for the review/dedupe layer.

data.title: Greenpill Network
data.notes: A global network of local chapters using crypto tools to fund and coordinate public goods per the article; same org already registered as a resource from types-of-gatherings.md ingestion.

data.title: Giveth
data.notes: Zero-platform-fee crypto donation platform, peer-to-peer wallet-to-wallet; running since 2016; per the article's headline stats, over 8,100 projects, roughly $5.7M in donations, and nearly 26,000 givers (a point-in-time snapshot, not necessarily current). Supports recipient addresses across Ethereum Mainnet, Gnosis Chain, Polygon, Polygon zkEVM, Stellar, Celo, Optimism, Solana, Arbitrum, Base, and Ethereum Classic.

data.title: DeVouch
data.notes: "A system for members of reputable organizations in the Ethereum ecosystem to vouch for or flag projects that are looking to raise funding" (quoted in the article). Decentralizes Giveth's project verification: trusted verifiers issue on-chain vouches worth 1, 3, or 30 points by tier; 3 points unlocks GIVpower boost, 30 points unlocks donor GIVbacks eligibility. No standalone URL given in this article.

data.title: Superfluid
data.notes: Protocol that streams tokens by the second rather than in one-off chunks; powers Giveth's recurring-donation "Stream Balance" feature, currently on Optimism or Base only, with ETH, OP, DAI, USDC, and GIV eligible per the article. No standalone URL given in this article.

data.title: Mobile wallets supported by Silvi (MetaMask, Valora, Opera MiniPay)
data.notes: Article names three wallet options a planter connects to Silvi to receive payment: MetaMask, Valora ("easy for beginners"), and Opera MiniPay ("simple mobile option"). Grouped as one resource entry since the article treats them as interchangeable payment-receiving options rather than distinct subjects of discussion.

data.title: Gardens v2 (1Hive)
data.notes: Conviction-voting DAO framework with covenant-based dispute resolution via Celeste; live on Gnosis Chain, Optimism, Arbitrum, Base, Polygon, and Celo per article.

data.title: Carbonmark
data.notes: Suggested in the article's "Try This" exercise as a place to browse real, individually-tracked carbon credits.

data.title: KlimaDAO
data.notes: URL is copied as printed in the article's reference list (klimaDAO.com); worth double-checking at review time against the project's canonical domain.

data.title: M-Pesa (East African mobile money)
data.notes: Named as a real-world fungibility analogy (mobile money units are interchangeable 1:1); no URL given in the article so link_status is unresolved rather than invented.

data.title: Argent
data.notes: Cited in the article as a "popular Ethereum social recovery wallet" — guardians (3-5 trusted contacts) can collectively help recover a lost wallet; adding a guardian is as simple as entering their address or name.

data.title: Safe (formerly Gnosis Safe)
data.notes: Cited in the article as "the most widely used multi-sig solution for DAOs and organisations." Recommended for treasury management with 3-of-5 or 4-of-7 threshold configurations depending on organization size, plus time-locks (24-48 hours) for large transfers.

data.title: L2Fees.info (live layer-2 transaction cost tracker)
data.what_it_is: A live tracker of real-time transaction costs across Optimism, Arbitrum and other layer-2 networks, cited to show that L2 fees are typically a fraction of a cent.

data.title: ReFi Medellín
data.notes: Colombia's first ReFi node, launched April 2023 with two founders (named in the article and its cited source: Tereza Bízková and Juan Giraldo), growing to a roughly seven-person team and ~150-person community within months. Cited as the article's worked example of starting tiny and growing through partnerships with existing local organizations (PlatoHedro, impactMarket) rather than building from scratch. Named individuals are reproduced here only as already publicly cited in the article's own source (a public Medium interview); see the companion public-use-boundary object for reuse guidance.

data.title: ReFi Cartagena
data.notes: A ReFi node cited as an example of a tight core founding team: four named team leaders per the article's cited source (a public grant report) — Daniela, Ximena, and Diana Monclou plus Fabio Anaya. Named individuals are reproduced here only as already publicly cited in the article's own source; see the companion public-use-boundary object for reuse guidance.

data.title: Safe (multisig wallets)
data.notes: Article's recommended tool for a node treasury: a 2-of-3 multisig so funds need at least two approvals to move, named as the "Stretch" action item and as one of the two node-specific no-single-point-of-failure rules (at least two people on the multisig).

data.title: ReFi DAO Local Node Incubator
data.notes: A 15-week beta cohort run by ReFi DAO with over 100 participants and 25-plus attending weekly, scoring 9.4/10 on recommendation, per the article's cited retrospective. Named alongside GreenPill Network as existing support a new founding team can plug into rather than inventing the playbook alone.

data.title: BrightID
data.notes: Named under Sybil Resistance measures as a proof-of-humanity tool to prevent one person creating multiple identities to gain extra votes; no URL given in this article.

data.title: Infinite Giving
data.notes: Described in the article as the "simple" option, good fit for small organisations. URL not given in article; link_status left unresolved pending verification.

Captured faithfully as named, flagged unresolved for a human to verify or correct rather than silently dropped or silently "fixed."

data.title: Safe (multisig wallet)
data.notes: Formerly Gnosis Safe. Article recommends a 3-of-5 multisig for even the lightest "Collective" model as a low-cost way to remove single-person custody risk before any legal wrapper exists. (See also multisig- setup.md for a dedicated deep-dive on multisig configuration, ingested separately in this batch.)

data.title: Open Collective
data.notes: Fiscal-hosting platform letting an unincorporated group raise and spend money transparently under a host (e.g. Open Source Collective, Open Collective Europe) without registering a legal entity — presented as a way to get most of a cooperative's benefits before incorporating.

data.title: CoinTracker
data.notes: Named in "Your Action Steps" as a crypto tax tool that automates the hard parts of tracking transactions.

data.title: Koinly
data.notes: Named in "Your Action Steps" alongside CoinTracker as a crypto tax tool that automates transaction tracking.

data.title: Gitcoin Grants
data.notes: Runs funding rounds using quadratic funding; current rounds (GG24 cycle, per the article) mix QF with other allocation mechanisms by domain.

data.title: Giveth
data.notes: Zero-fee crypto donation platform; article notes it supports recurring donations streamed via Superfluid on Optimism and Base.

data.title: Endaoment
data.notes: On-chain 501(c)(3) / donor-advised-fund platform; lets crypto donors give tax-deductibly if the node has charitable status or a fiscal sponsor. Creating a fund is free; donors pay a one-time 1.5% admin fee.

data.title: Juicebox
data.notes: Programmable on-chain treasury and fundraising tool; per the article, V4 deploys across Ethereum, Arbitrum, Base, and OP Mainnet.

data.title: Octant
data.notes: Public-goods funding driven by GLM staking and recurring epochs; cited in the article as "useful context on how on-chain funders allocate," not otherwise discussed in the body text.

data.title: Snapshot
data.notes: Described as the most widely used DAO voting platform: gasless voting, flexible voting strategies, off-chain IPFS storage; Snapshot X (2025) added fully on-chain voting on Starknet at lower cost.

data.title: Tally
data.notes: Described as the rigorous on-chain governance option, built on the OpenZeppelin Governor framework, handling governance for protocols managing billions in assets; offers immutable records, automatic execution, and delegation tracking. Article does not give a URL directly (no reference-list entry for Tally); URL left unresolved rather than invented.

data.title: Gnosis Safe
data.notes: Described as the standard DAO treasury tool: multi-signature wallet securing billions of dollars across millions of accounts, M-of-N approval, multi-chain support (20+ networks), hardware wallet compatibility.

data.title: Coordinape
data.notes: Used by 100+ DAOs including Bankless and Yearn Finance per the article; contributors allocate "GIVE" recognition tokens to peers, and allocated tokens determine payment distribution — a peer-to-peer alternative to manager-decided compensation.

data.title: Aragon
data.notes: Described as one of the first no-code DAO creation platforms, offering templates for governance structures. Article gives no URL in its reference list; not invented here.

Flagging for the curator to consider cross-linking rather than letting each article redefine the distinction independently.

data.title: Reviewed pages silently rot (silent drift) — maturity needs an expiry mechanism
data.interpretation: The article names "silent drift" (reviewed content going stale while still trusted) alongside stagnation and reactive overcorrection as the Toolkit's own named failure modes, with the governing rule "a signal is not a conclusion." It proposes two concrete mitigations worth evaluating for this framework's own K1 model: (1) expiry-by-date — a rule that demotes "Maintained" pages older than N months back to "Reviewed" until re-checked; (2) compost-not-delete — mark wrong-but-historically-useful content Deprecated with a pointer to its replacement rather than erasing it.

data.title: Format determines outcome more than topic — and open house is the best burnout defense
data.interpretation: Two reusable patterns worth carrying into any future local-node-onboarding track: (1) the same topic run through a different container produces a different outcome (a lecture on governance produces passive listeners; a fishbowl discussion on the same topic produces engaged co-thinkers), so format should be chosen deliberately, not defaulted to; (2) among all the formats in this guide, the recurring open house is named explicitly as the single best burnout defense for a node host (low cost, high consistency, keeps the node visible between bigger events) — worth surfacing as a starter recommendation whenever a node onboarding track is built.

data.title: Building a Minimum Viable Node (8-week MVN roadmap)
data.audience: regen organizers ready to launch a local node
data.starting_context: An organizer with community energy and prior exposure to other nodes' playbooks, facing the temptation to build a token, treasury, governance framework, and constitution before anyone can join — the pattern the article says burns out good organizers within three months.
outcome: A working minimum viable node: a shared one-sentence purpose, a way to track value, and five to ten people who reliably show up.
Real signal on whether the idea has legs, gathered in eight weeks instead of sunk months.

A concrete trigger table for when (and only when) to add technology — ledger software, lightweight roles, Snapshot voting, a Safe multisig — so complexity is added because coordination is straining, not to look serious.
deployment_checks: shared purpose statable in one sentence by the whole founding crew
a way to track value in place (spreadsheet, paper ledger, or hOurworld)
five to ten people who show up when it is raining, not just "interested"
failure_modes: Planning forever instead of running one real exchange — "this is where most nodes die."
Adding blockchain/DAO tooling (token, on-chain governance, legal entity) before human coordination has actually started to strain.
Running out of the funding needed to keep the lights on, even with a sound model and community support (the Bristol Pound/Bristol Pay precedent cited in the article).
Treating heavyweight legacy DAO frameworks (e.g. the older DAOstack/ Alchemy stack) as a starting line rather than a later destination.

data.title: First 90 Days: Local Node Playbook
data.audience: aspiring ReFi local-node organizers starting a place-based community
data.starting_context: A city, a handful of interested people, and no treasury, token, or incorporated entity yet.
outcome: days 1-30 — convene: find people already doing the work, host one small gathering (not a conference), reach a named core group of 3-5 people who showed up twice
days 31-60 — distribute the work: rotate facilitation and roles (events, partnerships, notes) so no single person is load-bearing; run a sustainable monthly rhythm
days 61-90 — fund carefully: only pursue funding (e.g. Gitcoin Grants) once there's a real group and a track record of a few events
deployment_checks: does a named core group of 3-5 repeat attendees exist before any incorporation/fundraising step?
are roles (events, partnerships, notes/follow-up) explicitly rotated rather than held by one person?
is the funding round (e.g. Gitcoin) walked through with the community beforehand (Gitcoin Passport, payout timing, gas fees)?
failure_modes: treating the node launch like a product launch (fundraising/token/ treasury before relationships exist)
one person carrying all coordination work until burnout stalls the node (per Commons Social Change Library's burnout research)
fundraising before a track record exists, creating a chicken-and-egg gap given multi-month grant payout timelines

data.title: Local Node Gathering Cadence
data.audience: local-node organizers (ReFi DAO / GreenPill Network chapter stewards)
data.starting_context: starting or currently running a regen local node, deciding what to actually do when people show up
outcome: a sustainable weekly/monthly/quarterly gathering rhythm matched to the node's current stage
reduced organizer burnout from over-ambitious calendars
decisions made transparently enough that even people who disagree stay engaged
deployment_checks: has the node named its current stage honestly (pre-formation / early formation / active operations / growth / renewal)?
is there a single owner for the recurring low-effort touchpoint (open house), not a committee?
are decision proposals circulated at least a week ahead of a town hall?
failure_modes: turning a relationship-building meal into a decision-making meeting ("while we're all here, let's just quickly...")
defaulting to lecture-mode for educational gatherings instead of hands-on/peer formats
running an ambitious high-effort calendar that burns out the host
skipping the informal-relationship layer and going straight to governance
data.notes: Synthesized from the article's "Choosing the Right Format" stage table and rhythm guidance into a guided-pathway object (track schema), since the article itself functions as exactly that: a stage-matched sequence of options for a local node, not a single deployment.

data.caution: Repeated visibility across directories, grants, analytics, registries or media can look like corroboration even when sources reuse the same self-reported information.
data.safe_working_language: Treat cross-platform presence as a relationship signal. Trace original sources and identify genuinely independent evidence.

data.title: Accessibility can be completed before publication

data.title: Community-centered alternatives are inherently inclusive
data.claim: Community-centered alternatives are inherently inclusive
data.caution: Communities contain differences and power inequalities involving caste, gender, class, disability, age, ethnicity and other structures.
data.safe_working_language: Review who defines the community, who participates, who benefits, who bears burdens and who can dissent or leave.

data.title: Connectivity is inherently empowering
data.claim: Connectivity is inherently empowering
data.caution: Connectivity can support rights and livelihoods but can also introduce surveillance, extraction, platform dependency, misinformation and unwanted social change.
data.safe_working_language: Assess connectivity alongside community goals, ownership, governance, safety, cultural fit, ecological effects and the right to refuse.

data.title: DAO metadata interoperability establishes governance transparency
data.claim: DAO metadata interoperability establishes governance transparency
data.caution: Shared metadata can improve discovery but may not reveal actual power, informal influence, conflicts, or decision quality.
data.safe_working_language: DAOstar and EIP-4824 support common metadata and discoverability; they do not certify transparent or legitimate governance.

data.title: Forum discussion equals ratified governance
data.claim: Forum discussion equals ratified governance
data.caution: Forum posts, call notes, and proposals preserve valuable field memory but may remain exploratory or contested.
data.safe_working_language: Record authorship, date, proposal status, decision path, and implementation evidence separately.

data.title: Generative and extractive systems are cleanly separable
data.claim: Generative and extractive systems are cleanly separable
data.caution: Real organizations often contain mixed incentives, value flows, labor arrangements, and ecological effects.
data.safe_working_language: Treat generative/extractive as an inquiry lens and document specific value flows, harms, and benefits.

data.title: High average accuracy means an AI system is safe or fair
data.claim: High average accuracy means an AI system is safe or fair
data.caution: Aggregate performance can conceal severe subgroup disparities, threshold effects and unequal consequences.
data.safe_working_language: Report disaggregated performance and institutional consequences; do not infer fairness from aggregate accuracy.

data.title: More information always improves system performance
data.claim: More information always improves system performance
data.caution: Information can aid coordination but may also create overload, surveillance, gaming, conflict or unequal power.
data.safe_working_language: Improved information flows may help when they are timely, usable, trusted, rights-respecting and connected to action.

data.title: Open source makes a civic platform publicly accountable
data.claim: Open source makes a civic platform publicly accountable
data.caution: Source visibility supports inspection and reuse but does not guarantee understandable governance, inclusive contribution, security, or public control.
data.safe_working_language: State the license, maintainers, hosting, governance, contribution process, auditability, and practical accessibility separately.

data.title: Ostrom’s natural-resource design principles can be directly applied to knowledge commons
data.claim: Ostrom’s natural-resource design principles can be directly applied to knowledge commons
data.caution: Knowledge and information differ from many biophysical common-pool resources, and GKC explicitly cautions against treating IAD or design principles as automatic starting points or conclusions.
data.safe_working_language: Use Ostrom as an important lineage while applying the GKC framework’s distinct empirical questions to knowledge, data and information.

data.title: Producer or beneficiary counts demonstrate equitable livelihood gains
data.claim: Producer or beneficiary counts demonstrate equitable livelihood gains
data.caution: Counts do not reveal income distribution, prices, debt, gendered control, labor burden or unequal value capture.
data.safe_working_language: State the reported count and separately identify what benefit means and how it is distributed.
